# New Hampshire — Election Directives, Guidance & Procedure Manuals

Dataset: State Election Rules and Guidance. Official guidance content for New Hampshire, compiled for the VB Election Desk knowledge base. Every section below cites the official source it was captured from and the publisher's own currency statement; sources were verified as official publications before inclusion.
Sections: 1

## New Hampshire Election Procedure Manual, 2026-2027 edition (RSA 652:22)

- **Publisher:** New Hampshire Secretary of State (with the advice and approval of the Attorney General)
- **Category:** manual
- **Registered source:** https://mm.nh.gov/files/uploads/sos/docs/nhsos-2026-epm-complete-book-remediated.pdf
- **Listed as current at:** https://www.sos.nh.gov/elections
- **Currency (publisher's statement):** Cover letter (PDF p. 3): 'NEW HAMPSHIRE SECRETARY OF STATE / To the Election Officials of New Hampshire: August 2026 ... This year, we have worked to streamline the Manual which reduced its overall length.' No month/day beyond 'August 2026' is given, so currency_date uses the first of that month.
- **Note:** Both www.sos.nh.gov and mm.nh.gov return an Akamai 'Access Denied' 403 to automated clients, for HTML pages and plain static asset paths alike, so this manual is captured from the Internet Archive's snapshot of the exact official URL (approved 2026-09-10). The snapshot used is 2026-09-04, of the August 2026 edition the Secretary of State lists as current.
- **Note:** Captured as one record: the manual is a single 301-page document with no rule-style section numbering to split on.
- **Note:** The Secretary of State's memos and updates issued between editions are not on the public web — the manual's own Memo/Updates Tracking Table says the current table lives in the Statewide Voter Registration System under 'Help > Instructions', which requires credentials.
- Note: this manual also appears in the Pollworker Guides dataset.

Memo/Updates Tracking Table 
Use this table to track memos and updates issued by the Secretary of State and the Attorney General. The 
Elections Help Desk staff will maintain a current “Updates Tracking Table” in the Statewide Voter 
Registration System (“SVRS”) “Help,” “Instructions.” To verify that you have received all the memos and 
updates issued since the publication of the manual, check the table in the SVRS.

NEW HAMPSHIRE 
SECRETARY OF STATE 
To the Election Officials of New Hampshire: August 2026 
Here in the Granite State, our state’s democracy thrives under the guardianship of our neighbors 
and friends. Local election officials are the backbone of local, state, and federal elections, and 
New Hampshire has a long track record of successful elections because of you. I appreciate your 
time, patience, and dedication to the people of New Hampshire. 
This year, we have worked to streamline the Manual which reduced its overall length. That said, 
we continue to incorporate your feedback from training sessions and direct conversations. We 
want to ensure you have all the information you need to feel comfortable in your positions and to 
carry out your duties effectively. 
The Secretary of State’s Office is here to answer your questions, listen to your feedback, and 
guide you in your positions as local election officials. We will continue to hammer home the 
message we believe in wholeheartedly: local and state election officials are your trusted sources 
of election information. 
Sincerely, 
David M. Scanlan 
Secretary of State

Preface 
This book is the Election Procedure Manual, prepared by the Secretary of State with the advice and 
approval of the Attorney General pursuant to RSA 652:22. It should be used in conjunction with the 
Secretary of State’s website at https://sos.nh.gov/, training resources provided to Clerks and Supervisors 
through SVRS, as well as Memos, Webinars, and other training provided to Moderators, Clerks, 
Supervisors of the Checklist, Boards of Selectmen, and other local School District and Village District 
election officials. 
The Manual begins with a “What is New” section describing changes in election laws since the 2024 
Manual was published. After that, the document is arranged in three core parts: Part 1, Elections from Start 
to Finish; Part 2, Duties of Election Officials by Office; and an Appendix. It finishes with an index. 
Part 1, Elections from Start to Finish, describes all aspects of an election chronologically. Newer election 
officials should read this part first so that they can understand every aspect of the election process. Every 
role interacts with and affects the others, so an election official should aim to understand (even just at a 
high level) the duties of the other offices. 
Part 2, Duties of Election Officials by Office, is designed for both new and experienced officials. For new 
officials, once they read Part 1, they can drill down in Part 2 on the precise and comprehensive duties 
required of them. For experienced officials who may not want to read all of Part 1, they can focus on their 
section in Part 2 to refresh their understanding of election law requirements for that office. 
Part 3, the appendix, contains different types of resources for officials. First, it contains many of the forms, 
certificates, and affidavits commonly used in elections. Second, it offers a few helpful visual guides for 
things like a full list of reasons to reject an absentee ballot or how voters can prove their United States 
citizenship. And third, it contains several charts to assist officials in common areas like alphabet distribution 
for check-in tables or retention of records. Not all election related documents are in this Manual—there are 
many that change so frequently that including them here would be futile. For this reason, they can be 
obtained in SVRS Help Instructions by Clerks or Supervisors. 
Finally, there is an extensive index at the back of the Manual to assist readers in quickly locating answers 
to questions. We know that many officials use the Manual in paper form and often when an urgent need 
arises. Especially on a busy election day, the index is your best friend. 
While this document reflects a concentrated effort by the Secretary of State’s Office and the Attorney 
General’s Office to summarize and organize the election laws, it is not binding legal authority. The Election 
Procedure Manual is a resource and learning tool. The Manual is not a substitute for the relevant statutes 
or for legal advice. Court decisions and changes to the statutes made between printings of the Manual may 
change the election laws. Whenever uncertainty exists as to what action to take, we will make our best 
effort to assist you and you should consult your local legal counsel. 
The Attorney General’s Office enforces the election laws and serves the Secretary of State as legal 
counsel. However, if a local election official is sued, the local election official’s town or city legal counsel will 
represent the official. If disagreement exists as to proper procedure, consult with your jurisdiction’s local 
legal counsel before acting.

Acknowledgements 
This Manual has grown over the years and, as such, has many contributors. To name just a few: 
• The work done in the past by the volunteers from the New Hampshire City and Town 
Clerks’ Association continues to serve as the foundation for this Manual. 
• This version of the Manual builds off the tireless work of former General Counsel Orville 
“Bud” Fitch II, former Deputy Secretary of State Erin Hennessey, and Attorney Jennifer 
Coté, who substantially revised and improved the Manual in 2024. Although Bud and Erin 
have since departed the Secretary of State’s Office, their sacrifices and dedication live on 
and they are dearly missed. 
• The 2026 revisions are largely the work of Attorneys Jennifer Coté and Douglas Bruno and 
Deputy Secretary of State (and attorney) Brendan O’Donnell. They have humbly aimed 
to distill a busy two years of election law changes into one document.

Changes to Filing Nomination Paper s and 
Witnessing Affidavits – RSA 655:15, 28. 
New Requirement that Clerks Post Election 
Return Forms – RSA 659:73. 
House Bill 327 (2025) made two changes to the 
filing of nomination papers for primaries. First, 
nominations for state representatives and 
delegates to the state convention can now be filed 
with the secretary of state. Second, if a candidate 
files in person before a town clerk or their deputy, 
the clerk or deputy may now witness candidates’ 
affidavits of qualifications, whether or not they are 
notaries. 
The Secretary of State will not inform the 
municipalities directly, as filings for all state offices 
will be displayed on the Secretary of State’s 
website and updated daily. 
Note that assistant clerks cannot witness a 
candidate’s affidavit of qualifications—the law only 
permits clerks or their deputies to do this. 
Senate Bill 16 (2025) now requires city and town 
clerks to post election return forms within seven 
days of an election. They must be posted in the 
two places where the municipality regularly posts 
notices of its governing body meeting. This may 
include the main website or town/city social media 
accounts. The legislature did not include a 
minimum length of time for posting election 
returns. The Secretary of State recommends the 
forms be posted for at least 30 days. 
Note that t hese changes apply to both state and 
local elections. 
Public Body Meeting Minutes: Start/End Times 
and Clerk Name(s) – RSA 91-A:2. 
House Bill 265 (2025) imposes new changes to 
New Hampshire’s Right-to-Know Law. For meeting 
minutes, the person taking minutes must now 
record the start and end time of the meeting. The

Optional Three- Year Terms for Supervisors – 
RSA 41:46-a. 
House Bill 151 (2025) gives local legislative bodies 
the option of choosing a three- year term for 
supervisors. Under such a system, one supervisor 
would be elected every year over the three- year 
cycle. 
The legislative body for each municipality will vary 
depending on whether the municipality has 
adopted a charter establishing one of the optional 
forms of legislative body, such as representative 
town meeting, city or town council, mayor and 
council, or mayor and board of aldermen. For 
towns that have not adopted a charter and have 
the select board -town meeting form of 
government, the town meeting is the legislative 
body. 
Only a town’s legislative body may adopt a three-
year term for supervisors of the checklist. For a 
town that has the select board-town meeting form 
of government, the town’s select board cannot 
adopt the three-year term for supervisors, but the 
board may propose a warrant article to be voted 
on at the next annual town meeting. 
Optional Three- Year Terms for Moderators – 
RSA 41:1-a. 
House Bill 1113 (2026) gives voters in towns the 
option of choosing a three- year term for 
moderators. If the town has adopted an official 
ballot, the ballot question shall state: “Are you in 
favor of changing the term of the moderator from 
(here insert term option) years to (here insert term 
option) years, beginning with the expiration of the 
term of the current moderator?” If the town has not 
adopted an official ballot, the clerk shall cause the 
same question to be printed upon special ballots. 
If the ballot question passes, then at the next 
annual meeting when the current moderator’s term 
expires, the town shall elect a moderator for a 
three-year term. 
Preservation and Destruction of Tabulator 
Memory Cards – RSA 33-A:3-a. 
House Bill 270 (2025) made two key changes in 
relation to electronic ballot counting device 
programmed external storage devices. First, when 
a clerk receives the programmed storage devices 
from the vendor, the law now requires them to lock 
any freestanding devices— meaning not plugged 
and appropriately sealed into the ballot counting 
devices—in a safe. The dictionary defines the 
word “safe” as “a place or receptacle to keep 
articles (such as valuables) safe.” This could 
include traditional safes, locked filing cabinets or 
desks, or fireproof safes. The clerk must also 
maintain an activity log that lists the “who, what, 
and when” regarding access to the safe. The 
activity logs will be available in SVRS . Note that 
they are public documents just like activity logs for 
sealed ballot boxes. 
Second, the programmed external storage devices 
must now be retained after all elections, stored 
with the sealed ballots, and recorded on the sealed 
ballot boxes chain of custody log. For federal 
elections, store them for 22 months (or until the 
contest is settled/appeals have expired). For all 
other elections, store them for 60 days (or until the 
contest is settled/appeals have expired). Extra 
electronic ballot counting device external storage 
devices programmed for, but not used, during the 
election are exempt from preservation. 
House Bill 1298 (2026) added the requirement 
that, after the retention period, programmed 
external storage devices must be disposed of 
either by physically destroying the device or 
securely erasing all election-related data (election 
programming, vote tallies, and digital images). 
Electioneering – Clothing Items – RSA 652:16-
h. 
Senate Bill 43 (2025) made changes to the law 
regarding electioneering clothing items. The law 
defines electioneering as “visibly displaying or 
audibly disseminating information that a 
reasonable person would believe explicitly 
advocates for or against any candidate, political

party, or measure being voted.” RSA 652:16 -h. 
Electioneering includes wearing clothing or 
paraphernalia that displays “a candidate's name, 
likeness, or logo, a ballot measure's number, title, 
subject, or logo, a political party's name or logo, or 
any communication that a reasonable person 
would believe explicitly advocates for or against 
any candidate, political party, or measure.” RSA 
652:16-h. 
With the passage of Senate Bill 43, the statute now 
states that individuals who are eligible to vote or 
register to vote on election day who are unable to 
reasonably remove or cover such clothing may 
wear it while actively and expeditiously registering 
or voting. 
The dictionary defines “expeditiously” as “marked 
by or acting with prompt efficiency.” Here, that 
means the voter should be allowed to register to 
vote, check in, receive, mark, and cast their ballot, 
and then leave the polling location. As long as the 
voter conducts this process promptly —i.e., not 
lingering unnecessarily —they are acting 
expeditiously. Note that these voters must leave 
the building after voting but can remain in the 
designated electioneering areas outside of the 
building. They cannot be in the observation area. 
The word “reasonable” means “fair, proper, or 
moderate under the circumstances; sensible.” As 
this definition indicates, reasonability depends 
upon context. What is reasonable under some 
circumstances may not be for others. Ultimately, 
election officials must make a judgment call. 
Conducting Political Surveys Is Now 
Considered Electioneering – RSA 652:16-h. 
House Bill 340 (2026) amended RSA 652:16-h to 
include the following new example of conduct that 
constitutes electioneering: “organizing or 
conducting surveys that are expressly or primarily 
political, meaning that they have a format, 
questions, or other characteristics that clearly 
indicate a preference for one or more candidates 
or political parties in an election or one or more 
policies that are reasonably anticipated to be on 
the ballot or otherwise at issue in an election.” 
E-Poll Books Expanded to Town /School 
Sessions and Special Meetings – RSA 652:27. 
Senate Bill 43 (2025) now permits use of electronic 
poll books for check-in at town or school business 
or deliberative sessions as well as special 
meetings. Any town or city that received electronic 
poll book conditional use approval from the 
Secretary of State can now use them for check-in 
at town or school business or deliberative sessions 
as well as special meetings. 
Officials should continue to mark the alpha voter 
official checklist in parallel until electronic poll 
books receive official certification from the 
Secretary of State. Please refer to the conditional 
use letter you received from the Secretary of State. 
Voters Can Now Request Their Ballots Be 
Hand-Counted – RSA 656:42. 
House Bill 154 (2025) now allows voters to request 
that their ballot be hand -counted in a town/ward 
that uses an electronic ballot counting device. If a 
voter does so, they must be instructed to hand the 
ballot to the election official manning the electronic 
ballot counting device, who must place the ballot 
in the side- pocket for it to be hand- counted after 
the polls close. 
Polling locations that fit this description will need to 
have two ballot boxes that are properly labeled in 
the event a voter asked for their ballot to be hand-
counted. If the electronic ballot counting device 
goes down in the middle of the election, have an 
extra ballot box available for use. Only place hand 
count ballots into the auxiliary compartment. Place 
all other ballots into the separate ballot box. Once 
the electronic ballot counting device is operational, 
you can then run the ballots cast in the separate 
ballot box through the device. 
New Proof of Qualification Requirements for 
Absentee Registration – RSA 654:17. 
Senate Bill 218 (2025) changed the proof of voter 
qualification requirements for non-UOCAVA 
absentee voter registrations. Individuals seeking

to register absentee must now provide proof of the 
qualifications required for in- person registrations. 
Thus, absentee registrants shall provide 
documentation proving citizenship, age, domicile, 
and identity. Previously, absentee voter registrants 
were not required to provide proof of citizenship or 
age. The law also requires that if such registrants 
do not provide proof of the required qualifications, 
their applications shall be denied. However, a 
second bill that passed (HB464) does not require 
the registrant to provide proof of citizenship or age 
if they were previously registered in NH or are 
currently registered in another town/ward. This bill 
also revises the forms voters must submit with 
their proof of qualifications. 
If the person did not provide proof of citizenship, 
the election official receiving the application should 
first confirm in SVRS or other official records 
whether the person is currently or was previously 
registered to vote in a New Hampshire town or 
ward. If the person failed to provide satisfactory 
proof of citizenship or age and the election official 
cannot confirm that the pers on is a currently, or 
previously, registered voter, or if the person failed 
to provide satisfactory proof of identity or domicile, 
then the person’s absentee voter registration 
application must be denied. The election official 
should record the reason the absentee registration 
was rejected on the form. The official should 
promptly notify the person that their absentee 
registration was rejected and provide the reason 
the absentee registration was rejected. After 
sending this notice, the official should save a copy 
of the notice with the rejected absentee 
registration documents. 
If the clerk receives an absentee ballot application 
and the voter is not a registered voter and does not 
submit a photo ID or notarization, then send the 
absentee not registered to vote package. Do NOT 
send an absentee ballot. 
Changes to Timeline for Absentee Ballot 
Applications – RSA 657:6. 
House Bill 288 (2025) made changes to the timing 
of the non -UOCAVA absentee ballot application 
process. Clerks may now only accept such 
applications postmarked or received within six 
months of the election for which the absentee 
ballot is being requested. 
If clerks receive a non -UOCAVA absentee ballot 
application prior to the six-month cutoff, it will need 
to be rejected if the application was not received 
or post marked within 6 months of the election for 
which the absentee ballot was requested. In 
accordance with RSA 657:16, the clerk shall notify 
the applicant within 7 days of not accepting the 
application. In that notice, the clerk should include 
a new absentee ballot application form and identify 
the earliest date an application can be posted or 
received. Best practice is to stamp or mark the 
application with the date received and a note that 
it was rejected. Retain the rejected application and 
notice, as these are not recorded in SVRS. 
If the clerk receives a non- UOCAVA absentee 
ballot application before the six -month cutoff but 
the voter needs to register, send the voter the 
absentee voter registration materials and also 
notify the applicant that the application was 
rejected because it was not received or 
postmarked within 6 months of the election for 
which the absentee ballot was requested. See 
RSA 657:16. 
Optional Outer Envelope for Hand Delivery – 
RSA 657:7, 16. 
Under Senate Bill 218 (2025), an absentee ballot 
only needs to be placed in the outer envelope if it 
is mailed to the clerk. An absentee voter who hand 
delivers their absentee ballot (properly sealed in 
the affidavit envelope (A)) and supporting 
documentation does not need to place t hese 
documents in the outer envelope. SB 218 also 
changes the affidavit envelope (form A), adding 
lines for the voter’s printed name and address. 
Clerks will therefore need to obtain new affidavit 
envelopes (note that for local elections they must 
be purchased and do not come from the Secretary 
of State’s Office). 
To avoid the situation where the election official

affidavit was received from, the ballot should be 
rejected. 
Another option exists if there is only one 
outstanding voter listed on the absentee ballot 
report at the end of the day —election officials are 
permitted to determine by process of elimination 
that the ballot must belong to the voter. 
This process may also interact with absentee 
registration. If an authorized delivery agent returns 
a voter’s absentee affidavit envelope to the clerk 
without an outside envelope and the voter was 
marked as “registering to vote,” then open the 
envelope, remove the forms, close and seal the 
envelope, and record on the envelope the date, 
time, clerk’s initials, and reason for opening. 
New Identity Verification Requirements for 
Absentee Ballot Applications – RSA 657:17-c. 
Senate Bill 287 (2025) adds an identity verification 
requirement for non-UOCAVA absentee ballot 
applications. Applicants can provide sufficient 
verification in one of several ways: (1) providing a 
copy of the person’s photo identification that meets 
the requirements of RSA 659:13, II(a); (2) 
personally presenting photo identification to the 
clerk or their designee that meets the requirements 
of RSA 659:13, II(a); or (3) having their signature 
on the absentee ballot application notarized. You 
cannot issue an absentee ballot unless an 
applicant provides one of the three identity 
verification methods. 
Note that the photo identification must be included 
“with the absentee ballot application” or 
“personally present[ed].” This means that you 
cannot accept an absentee ballot application 
without a copy of the photo identification and have 
the individual email it to you separately. Moreover, 
the notarization must be of the application itself — 
it cannot be some other document. 
Do NOT send absentee ballots unless the voter 
meets the requirements above. The law states that 
“No absentee ballot shall be issued unless one of 
the verification methods under paragraph I has 
been satisfied.” 
Notarized absentee ballot application forms can be 
accepted via email or fax, and voters can use the 
remote notarization process. More information on 
that process can be found on our website. See 
https://www.sos.nh.gov/electronic-and-remote-
notarization 
If a voter sends in multiple absentee ballot 
requests for different elections and includes only 
one copy of their photo identification, make copies 
so that each application has a copy of the 
identification. Notarized applications do not work 
the same way, because the notary must witness 
the signature. Applications that are not notarized 
cannot be accepted. 
For nursing homes, remember that nursing home 
administrators can verify the voter’s identity. They 
can therefore assist nursing home residents by 
providing an oath or affirmation to the notary who 
can then notarize the application. The clerk can be 
the notary who does this, as long as they verify the 
nursing home administrator’s identity and 
determine the administrator is a credible witness. 
Checklists Must Now Be Verified Annually – 
RSA 654:39. 
Senate Bill 221 (2025) shortens the timeline for 
verification of the checklist. Beginning in 2026, 
supervisors must now verify the checklist annually. 
It also lengthens the look-back period. Voters who 
have voted in any election within the past five 
years preceding the annual v erification will be

Current or Prior Registration In NH Is Proof of 
Citizenship – RSA 654:12. 
House Bill 464 (2025) made several changes to 
the proof of citizenship requirements. Applicants 
who were formerly registered in any New 
Hampshire town or ward or are currently registered 
in a different town or ward in New Hampshire do 
not need to provide proof of citizenship or age. 
They only need to prove their current or prior 
registration. 
If the election official has access to SVRS, then 
they can verify the voter’s current or prior 
registration by searching for the voter in “inquiries.” 
A marked checklist can also be used. 
Session for Corrections in Local Elections No 
Longer Must be on a Saturday – RSA 669:5. 
HB1325 (2026) eliminates the requirement that 
Supervisors hold their session for correction on a 
Saturday 6 to 13 days before the election. They 
now must hold the session using the same timeline 
as for state elections, following the process in RSA 
654:25—654:31. This means they must hold the 
session 6 to 13 days before the election. 
Elimination of Student ID for Use in 
Registration or Obtaining a Ballot – RSA 654:12 
& 659:13. 
HB323 (2026) eliminates the use of student 
identification cards for voter registration and 
obtaining a ballot. Students will need to use other 
approved forms of identification, such as drivers or 
non-drivers identification cards issued by DMV, 
federal form s of identification, or United States 
military identification cards. 
Changes to Identity Verification by Election 
Officials with Personal Knowledge of 
Individual – RSA 659:13. 
House Bill 317 (2026) removes the option of an 
election official verifying a person’s identity when 
they seek to register to vote (except for nursing 
home residents). Voters seeking to register must 
now present one of the proofs of identity listed in 
RSA 659:13. 
An election official can, however, verify a 
registered voter’s identity when they arrive on 
election day to obtain a ballot. The bill clarifies that 
a moderator, clerk, supervisor, or selectman may 
verify the voter’s identity if they personally know 
the voter. That election official must complete an 
Attestation of Identity For A Registered Voter On 
Election Day which must also be witnessed by the 
clerk or moderator. Note that a clerk or moderator 
cannot personally verify a voter and also witness 
their own verification. It requires two election 
officials. 
Note that the Secretary of State’s Office interprets 
this bill as including assistant election officials and 
pro tempore positions. 
State Primary Moved to June Beginning in 2028 
– RSA 653:8. 
House Bill 481 (2026) moved the state primary to 
the second Tuesday in June every even-numbered 
year (instead of September). This will not take 
effect until 2028. 
In line with this change, the legislature moved back 
various filing and meeting requirements:

• The deadline to change party affiliation is now 
the first Friday in March. RSA 654:34, IV. 
• The filing period for declarations of candidacy 
is now from the first Friday in March to the 
Friday of the following week. RSA 655:14. 
• The deadline to file supplementary primary 
petitions (if the original was rejected) is now the

Polling Place Size Limitation in Presidential 
Elections – RSA 658:11-a. 
Senate Bill 103 (2026) requires that, in any general 
election for the office of the President of the United

Qualifications for Obtaining Non- Driver ID

Clarification of Moderator Duties When 
Disqualified – RSA 659:58. 
House Bill 1266 (2026) now allows moderators to

related to the tabulation of votes. 
Changes to Appointment Process for 
Vacancies in Party Nominations – RSA 655:32, 
I. 
House Bill 1381 (2026) makes changes to the

deadline for the person designated by the party

the Secretary of State’s Office is now within 10 
business days following the close of the filing

person to file an affidavit of qualifications to the

Voter Registration Overview 
Voter registration in New Hampshire ensures that 
all qualified citizens can exercise their right to vote. 
In order to register to vote, applicants must be: 
1. At least 18 years of age; 
a. If registering to vote prior to an election, the 
applicant must be at least 18 years of age 
by the date of the next election. 
b. If registering to vote on the day of the 
election, the applicant must be at least 18 
years of age on that day. 
2. A United States citizen; 
3. Domiciled in the town, ward, or unincorporated 
place in which they are registering to vote; and 
4. Not otherwise disqualified to vote: 
a. Under Part I, Article 11 of the State 
Constitution, “ [n]o person shall have the 
right to vote under the constitution of this 
state who has been convicted of treason, 
bribery or any willful violation of the election 
laws of this state or of the United States” 
unless that person’s right to vote is later 
restored by the New Hampshire Supreme 
Court; or 
b. Under RSA 607 -A:2, I(a), a person 
sentenced for a felony from the time of his 
or her sentence until his or her release 
(which includes probation or parole). 
The voter registration form is prescribed by statute. 
RSA 654:7. 
An applicant can register to vote several ways: 
1. Registering at their town or city clerk’s 
office; 
2. Registering at a public session of the 
supervisors of the checklist, including 
publicly noticed voter registration drives at 
which a quorum of the supervisors of the 
checklist are present; 
3. Registering at a voter registration intake 
drive (a clerk, the clerk’s deputy or other 
staff, and supervisors (with approval of a 
majority of the board) can participate in a 
voter registration application intake event 
that is not a public session of the 
supervisors); 
4. Completing an absentee voter registration, 
if qualified to do so; or 
5. Registering on election day with the 
supervisors of the checklist. Federal and 
state law require that registration records 
on all voters be entered into a single 
statewide computerized voter registration 
system (“SVRS”). 52 U.S.C. § 21083; RSA 
654:45.

Supervisors of the Checklist 
Supervisors of the checklist are the election 
officials responsible for registering voters; 
removing voters who permanently move, die, or 
otherwise become disqualified; and preparing, 
posting, revising, and certifying the “checklist” of 
registered voters in their town or ward. Some cities 
call these officers the “board of registrars” instead, 
but both state law and this manual use the term 
“supervisors” to refer to the group collectively. RSA 
652:15. 
Supervisors are elected by the town or city ward in 
which they are domiciled. The board of supervisors 
in each town is composed of a minimum of three 
members who are legal voters in the town. The 
equivalent of the board of supervisors of the 
checklist of a town are called Registrars of Voters 
in some cities. Registrars are chosen in the 
manner prescribed by the city charter and have the 
authority granted by the charter. The default 
procedure for electing supervisors is to elect one 
supervisor every even numbered year for a term of 
six years. RSA 41:46 -a. Thus, there will be one 
supervisor elected every two years. The legislative 
body of the city or town may, however, adopt a 3 -
year term for supervisors, electing one each year 
over a three-year cycle. RSA 41:46-a. 
The “checklist” is a document maintained in each 
town and ward which contains certain information 
regarding every qualified voter registered in that 
town or ward. This information includes the voter’s 
full name, domicile address, mailing address, and 
party affiliation, if any. RSA 654:25. The checklist 
is produced through SVRS. It is regularly reviewed 
at public sessions by the supervisors, at which 
time the supervisors act on pending applications, 
address and name changes, requests for removal, 
in-state transfers, property transfers, national 
changes of address, annual checkli st verification, 
and death notices. RSA 654:27, 654:27-a. 
Supervisors are required to hold public sessions at 
least every 90 days.  Supervisors are also 
required to meet: (i) on the Tuesday before the 
beginning of the candidate filing period for a state 
election; (ii) on the day before the beginning of the 
candidate filing period for a local election; (iii) on 
the Friday before the beginning of the candidate 
filing period for a New Hampshire presidential 
primary election; (iv) six to 13 days before a stat e 
or local election; (v) during each state and local 
election; and (vi) when conducting the annual 
verification of the checklist. These mandatory 
sessions can fulfill the requirement to meet at least 
every 90 days. Postings of meetings must be done 
at least seven days prior to the meeting. RSA 
654:27-a. See Duties of Supervisors of the 
Checklist for in-depth guidance. 
Voter Registration Form 
Each person who seeks to register must fill out a 
voter registration form. The current version of the 
voter registration form can be found in SVRS Help 
Instructions. Be sure to use the most recent 
version from November 2024. Supervisors must 
ensure they have a sufficient supply of the correct 
version of these forms for themselves and the town 
or city clerk. 
D
ETERMINING AN APPLICANT’S QUALIFICATIONS 
Once an applicant completes the voter registration 
form, the clerk or supervisor must determine 
whether the applicant is legally qualified to vote in 
that town or ward. The ultimate determination of an 
applicant’s qualifications is a judgment that the 
supervisors of the checklist must make. An 
applicant must be placed on the checklist unless a 
majority of the supervisors agree that it is more 
likely than not that the applicant is not qualified. 
RSA 654:11. While the Secretary of State will 
assist in clarifying what these qualifications are, 
the supervisors must judge whether an applicant 
should be registered. 
All applicants must meet the following 
qualifications: 
1. Identity. 
An applicant must prove their identity to establish 
that the evidence used to prove age, citizenship, 
and domicile relates directly to the applicant.

Only one of the following may be used to prove 
identity: 
• A Photo driver’s license issued by any state or 
the federal government; 
• A United States passport, passcard, armed 
services identification, or other photo 
identification issued by the federal 
government; 
• 
• 
Photo identification issued by local or state 
government; 
Residents of a nursing home or similar facility 
may prove their identity through verification by 
the facility administrator or the administrator’s 
designee, provided that the 
administrator/designee also sign the voter 
registration application; or 
• Any other evidence that reasonably 
establishes that it is more likely than not that 
the person is who they claim to be. 
o Note: Through September 7, 2026, this 
can include verification of the person’s 
identity by the moderator or another 
election official. RSA 654:12, I(d)(4). 
However, effective September 8, 2026, 
RSA 654:12, I(d)(4) was amended to 
remove the option for an election official 
to verify a person’s identity when 
registering to vote. 
Note: a student identification card cannot be used 
to prove identity. 
These forms of identification are presumptive 
evidence of the identity of the applicant. 
2. Age. 
For those applicants registering prior to an 
election, the applicant must be at least 18 years of 
age by the date of the next election. This means 
that, for example, a 17-year-old who will turn 18 in 
October and therefore be eligible to vote in a 
November general election may not register until 
after the September primary. 
For those applicants registering on election day, 
the applicant must be at least 18 years of age on 
that date. 
Applicants can prove age with any reasonable 
documentation indicating their age. An applicant’s 
document to prove identity, for example, frequently 
states their age as well (for example, a passport or 
a driver’s license will display the applicant’s 
birthday) and can be used to prove age. Proof that 
the applicant is currently or was previously 
registered to vote also qualifies. This can be done 
through SVRS or other official documents, such as 
a current or marked checklist. 
3. Citizenship. 
The applicant must be a United States citizen. 
Permanent residents (i.e. green card holders) are 
not United States Citizens and are not qualified to 
vote in elections. 
Applicants can prove citizenship in one of the 
following ways: by providing documentary proof of 
citizenship, asking a local election official to verify 
citizenship through state databases, or completing 
a Qualified Voter Affidavit. 
A. Documentary Proof of Citizenship : An 
applicant may provide one of the following 
documents listing their current legal name to 
prove United States citizenship: 
• 
• 
• 
• 
• 
A Birth certificate; 
A United States passport or passport card; 
Naturalization papers; 
One of the four trusted traveler cards 
issued by the United States Customs & 
Border Protection, identifying the applicant 
as a U.S. citizen – Global Entry, NEXUS, 
SENTRI, and FAST cards; 
Proof that the applicant was previously or 
is currently registered to vote in a different 
town or ward in New Hampshire (such as a 
public or marked checklist from a New 
Hampshire municipality showing the 
applicant was or is registered to vote); 
• 
• 
United States Department of State 
Consular Report of Birth Abroad; 
United States Department of State

Certification of Birth Abroad; or 
• Other reasonable documentation which 
indicates the applicant is a United States 
citizen. 
o Note: a REAL -ID driver’s license or 
non-driver ID is not evidence of United

States citizen has to prove citizenship 
to obtain a REAL ID, non- citizens 
legally present in the U.S. may also

Permanent Residents with a green 
card or other appropriate visa. 
However, if a United States citizen 
obtained a REAL- ID from the N.H. 
Division of Motor Vehicles, that 
person’s citizenship may be verified 
using the DMV inquiry feature in SVRS. 
o Note: A Lawful Permanent Resident, or 
permanent resident card, often referred 
to as a ‘green’ card, is evidence that the 
applicant is not a U.S. citizen. Some 
green card holders become U.S. 
citizens through naturalization and will 
qualify to vote in U.S. elections. 
However, unless and until they become 
U.S. citizens, they are not permitted to 
register to vote or vote. 
B. Proving Citizenship with State Database 
Information 
If the applicant does not have documentary proof 
of citizenship, the applicant may authorize local 
election officials to conduct one of the following 
searches to confirm citizenship: 
• 
• 
• 
Searching the Statewide Voter Registration 
System to confirm the applicant was previously 
or currently registered to vote in any New 
Hampshire municipality; 
The Statewide Voter Registration System has 
New Hampshire Vital Records information 
regarding New Hampshire births. A search for 
this information may help prove citizenship for 
certain voters; or 
The Statewide Voter Registration System has 
information from the N.H. Division of Motor 
Vehicles regarding citizenship status for 
individuals who have obtained an N.H. Driver’s 
License or Non -Driver ID. A search of this 
information may help prove citizenship for 
certain voters. 
C. Qualified Voter Affidavit – Citizenship 
Citizenship may also be proven by completing a 
qualified voter affidavit attesting, subject to the 
penalties of voter fraud, that the applicant is a 
United States citizen but does not possess some 
or all of the documents necessary to prove 
citizenship. 
a. Note: Under prior state law, an applicant 
could complete a qualified voter affidavit to 
prove citizenship, age, or domicile. Although 
that law was repealed effective November 
11, 2024, a court order subsequently struck 
down the repeal of the qualified voter 
affidavit for citizenship only. Accordingly, a 
voter can use a qualified voter affidavit to 
prove citizenship, but they cannot use an 
affidavit to prove age, identity, or domicile. 
4. Domicile. 
The concept of domicile comes from New 
Hampshire’s constitution. It provides that “ every 
inhabitant of the state of 18 years of age and 
upwards shall have an equal right to vote in any 
election.” N.H. C
ONST. Pt. I, Art. 11. It then explains 
that “[e]very person shall be considered an 
inhabitant for the purposes of voting in the town, 
ward, or unincorporated place where he has his 
domicile.” Building off this, New Hampshire law 
defines domicile for voting purposes as “that one 
place where a person, more than any other place, 
has established a physical presence and 
manifests an intent to maintain a single continuous 
presence for domestic, social, and civil purposes 
relevant to participating in democratic self-
government.” RSA 654:1, I.

Determining an individual’s domicile is a question 
of fact. Based on the available evidence, is it more 
likely than not that the applicant has established a 
physical presence at the place claimed as 
domicile? If yes, is it more likely than not that the 
applicant has manifested an intent or has acted to 
maintain that one place, more than any other 
place, a continuous presence for domestic, social, 
and civil purposes relevant to participating in a 
democratic self-government? If the answer to both 
questions is “yes,” the applicant has satisfactorily 
proven their domicile for voting purposes. 
Primary Proof of Domicile : If an applicant 
possesses one of the following qualified 
documents identifying their name and address 
they claim as domicile, they must present the 
document when registering to vote: 
• 
• 
•

A New Hampshire driver’s license or

An applicant’s domicile is qualified for voter 
registration purposes even if the person living at 
that address is doing so unlawfully . An 
applicant who is living in a campground in violation 
of a local ordinance prohibiting use of the 
campground as principal residence/domicile may 
nonetheless register to vote using that domicile. 
Similarly, a person who is living in a park which 
does not allow camping or is on property in 
violation of a do not trespass order may 
nonetheless register to vote using that domicile. 
Such a person, even if convicted of violating an 
ordinance or law, does not lose the right to vote.

SING SVRS TO VERIFY CITIZENSHIP, A GE, 
DOMICILE, AND NAME CHANGES 
Effective January 1, 2026, changes in the law 
authorized the Department of Motor Vehicles and 
Vital Records Division to provide certain data 
within SVRS . This information includes motor 
vehicle driver’s license records as well as birth, 
death, marriage, civil union, civil union dissolution 
and divorce information. 
This means that applicants who do not have proof 
of citizenship, age, domicile, or name changes, 
may be verified in SVRS depending on the 
circumstance. It is important to note that this 
process will not work for all types of applicants. 
Applicants verified through this process must also 
fill out an Application for Confidential Verification of 
a New Hampshire Vital Record or DMV Record 
prior to any record being searched. This form is 
available in SVRS. 
Note: Clerks and supervisors are NOT permitted 
to conduct these searches unless the voter 
appears and signs the application. Clerks and 
supervisors who perform searches without a voter 
present in front of an election official may be 
referred to the Attorney General’s Office. 
To learn more, please visit SVRS Help Instructions 
and search for “SVRS Changes (HB464) – 
Guidance” and “Inquiry Instructions – Vital 
Records and DMV.”

court-approved name change) and will use any of 
the above documents to prove one of their voter 
qualifications, the applicant must present proof 
their legal name change that shows their prior

REE CERTIFIED COPY OF A VITAL RECORD FOR 
VOTER PURPOSES ONLY FOR PROOF OF CITIZENSHIP 
OR NAME CHANGES 
Applicants who do not have proof of citizenship or 
name changes may also obtain a free certified 
copy of a vital record from their town and city 
clerks’ offices. They will be printed on blue safety 
paper and have a raised seal. The certified copies 
can only be used when registering to vote and 
must be surrendered to the election official intaking 
the voter registration application. 
The free certified copies available for voter 
registration include New Hampshire birth, 
marriage, divorce, civil union, and civil union 
dissolution records. Applicants seeking a free 
certified copy must fill out an Application for a Free 
Certified Copy of a New Hampshire Vital Record 
for NH Voter Registration Form. This form can be 
found in SVRS.

and search for “Application for a Free Certified 
Copy of a NH Vital Record for Voter Registration 
Email Guidance.”

NHOUSED APPLICANTS 
The same requirements for domicile apply to all. 
An unhoused person has a right to register and 
vote in that town or ward where they, “more than 
any other place, ha[ve] established a physical 
presence and manifest[ed] an intent to maintain” 
their domicile. RSA 654:1. 
Keep in mind that a person who establishes 
domicile and becomes temporarily absent with the 
intention of returning does not lose their domicile. 
RSA 654:2, I. Additionally, domicile for the purpose 
of voting, once existing, continues to exist until 
another such domicile is gained. RSA 654:2, I. For 
unhoused persons, this means that a person who 
establishes domicile in a town or ward and 
subsequently becomes unhoused or temporarily 
resides in one or more other locations, that 
person’s domicile does not terminate until they 
have established a new domicile. 
An unhoused applicant’s domicile may be the 
street, parking lot, or park/woodland, for example, 
where the person lives/sleeps more than any other 
place. Do not deny a person who is otherwise 
qualified to vote from registering because they do 
not have a home. Request the applicant complete 
the Homeless Confirmation of Domicile attestation 
form, and identify a mailing address where the 
applicant can receive mail. Note: Unhoused 
persons may have many different living situations. 
If you have an applicant whose situation does not 
appear to be directly covered by the Homeless 
Confirmation of Domicile, reach out to the 
Secretary of State’s  Office or Attorney General 
Election Law Unit for assistance with the 
applicant’s voter registration. No person who is 
qualified to vote can be denied that right on the 
basis of being unhoused.

any one of the following is true:

icant is unable to register in person

The applicant is a victim of domestic violence

or is participating in the Attorney General ’s

The applicant is confined to a penal institution

Applicants must request the absentee voter 
registration affidavit and voter registration form 
from their town/city clerk. RSA 654:16. If an 
unregistered voter requests an absentee ballot 
application, the clerk must send the voter an 
absentee ballot along w ith the absentee 
registration package if the clerk has ballots. 
New Hampshire is exempt from the federal 
National Voter Registration Act (the “Motor Voter” 
law). If a federal motor voter postcard registration 
from someone who is absent or disabled, the clerk 
or the supervisors must send the applicant the 
materials required for a New Hampshire Absentee 
Voter Registration. If the applicant is not absent or 
disabled, they can be notified to come to the clerk’s 
office or a session of the supervisors to register in 
person. 
The New Hampshire legislature passed SB 218 
(2025), effective September 30, 2025, which 
changes the proof required for absentee voter 
registrations. Individuals seeking to register 
absentee must now provide the same proof of 
qualifications (citizenship, age, domicile, and 
identity) required as if they were registering in 
person. RSA 657:17-c. 
Note: a person previously registered to 
vote in New Hampshire or currently 
registered to vote in another town or ward 
is not required to provide proof of 
citizenship or age. RSA 654:12, I(a). If an 
absentee voter registration is received 
without proof of citizenship or age, check 
SVRS to determine if the applicant was 
previously or currently registered in 
another town or ward before denying the 
application. 
The town or city clerk must send Absentee Voter 
Registration Forms to anyone who requests them. 
The applicant must return the completed 
applications to the clerk, and the clerk shall provide 
the completed application to the supervisors of the 
checklist at or before their next session. See 
Duties of Clerk for in-depth guidance. 
These new proof of qualification requirements do 
not affect UOCAVA voters; federal and state law 
specifies the requirements for accepting FPCA 
forms. RSA 657:6. 
F
EDERAL OFFICE ONLY VOTERS (DOMICILED 
OUTSIDE THE U.S.) 
A Federal Office Only (“FOO”) voter’s ballot has 
only the offices of United States President, United 
States Senator, and Representative in Congress 
listed on it. A FOO Voter is neither a regular 
absentee voter nor a military voter (uniformed 
services voter) who is simply overseas. A FOO 
Voter is a person living outside the United States 
who no longer maintains a domicile in New 
Hampshire, but who had their last domicile before 
leaving the United States in New Hampshire. A 
child or legal dependent of a person qualified as a 
FOO voter and who is a United States citizen may 
also be a FOO voter even if they have never lived 
in the United States or New Hampshire. A person 
most recently domiciled in or registered to vote 
anywhere else in the United States does not 
qualify to vote in New Hampshire as a FOO voter. 
The voter must have a valid United States 
Passport or card of identity issued by the U.S. 
State Department. RSA 654:3, III. 
A voter is a FOO voter if they submit a Federal Post 
Card Application (“FPCA”) form with either of the 
following checked in the “Who are you?” section: 
•
 
• 
“
I am a U.S. citizen living outside the county, 
and my intent to return is uncertain;” or 
“I am a U.S. citizen living outside the country, 
and I have never lived in the United States.”

A voter living outside the United States may 
download a FPCA form from the Federal Voting 
Assistance Program: https://www.fvap.gov. Do not 
send a standard Voter Registration Form or 
Absentee Ballot Application to a voter reporting 
they live outside the United States. Clerk s should 
keep a copy of the completed FPCA and provide 
the original to the supervisors. Once registered, a 
FOO voter is eligible to vote for federal offices only. 
The Secretary of State prepares and provides 
clerks with a FOO absentee ballot for each state 
election where voters will vote in a federal election. 
A
BSENTEE WRITE-IN BALLOT 
An absent uniformed services voter, an absent 
voter temporarily residing outside the U.S., or a 
voter domiciled outside the U.S. who, due to 
requirements of military service or due to living in 
an isolated area outside the United States, is 
unlikely to hav e sufficient time to receive, mark, 
and return a regular absentee ballot may apply for 
both a regular and a write-in absentee ballot. RSA 
657:10-a. 
A voter qualified to vote by absentee write-in ballot 
may obtain an Official Federal Write- In Absentee 
Ballot (“FWAB”) from the U.S. Department of 
Defense website at https://www.fvap.gov. These 
FWABs must be accepted by moderators and 
clerks as official ballots, so long as there is a voter 
signature on the affidavit. Note: in order for a 
moderator and clerk to accept an FWAB, there 
must be an FPCA on file requesting a state 
absentee ballot. If the voter received assistance 
with voting and the name and signature of the 
person assisting is on the form, the signature is not 
required for a voter with a disability who is unable 
to sign the form. Count the absentee ballot if other 
requirements set forth above are satisfied. 
Changing Party Affiliation 
A registered voter may change their party 
affiliation any time the supervisors are in session, 
except between the first day of the filing period for 
a state or presidential primary and up to the day 
of the primary election. When a voter moves from 
one New Hampshire town to another, treat the 
voter as a new registrant for this purpose – all 
new registrants may choose any party affiliation, 
regardless of the voter’s party affiliation where the 
voter was previously registered. The law also 
authorizes city and town clerks to accept 
applications to change party affiliation, and the 
clerk will provide the party change request to the 
supervisors. 
U
NDECLARED VOTERS 
A voter may register to vote as a member of any 
recognized political party or as undeclared. 
Undeclared voters are not a member of any 
political party and are also called unaffiliated 
voters. RSA 654:34. An unaffiliated voter may 
declare an affiliation at the primary and may vote 
on the ballot of their chosen party. 
Undeclared voters may declare their affiliation at a 
primary election and vote on the ballot of their new 
party. Voters may, after voting and before leaving 
the polling place, change back to undeclared by 
completing the Undeclared Voters Election Day 
Party Affiliation Change Form or signing the 
Undeclared Voters Re-Registration List which was 
prepared for the purpose of recording party 
changes back to undeclared. RSA 654:34, II(b) & 
V. This form is available in SVRS Help Instructions. 
The voter may also change back to undeclared 
after the election at the clerk’s office or a session 
of the supervisors. RSA 654:34. 
Note: a polling place that uses the 
Undeclared Voters Re-Registration List 
should still have some of the forms 
available because the list will not include 
any election- day voters who register as 
undeclared before taking a party primary 
ballot. 
Voters who register to vote as a member of a party 
and vote on that party’s ballot at a primary election 
shall not fill out a form to change their party status 
to unaffiliated on primary election day. RSA 
654:34, III & V.

their preferred candidate on their declared 
affiliation’s ballot. If this candidate is on a different 
party’s ballot, the vote will not count as a vote in 
the other party’s total. Rather, the write-in vote will 
count as a vote for that candidate in the party the 
voter received a ballot for. 
For example, a voter writes in “John Doe” on the 
Party A ballot for governor. John Doe is a 
candidate for Party B’s nomination. This voter’s 
write-in vote for John Doe will not be counted in the 
votes for John Doe on the Party B ballot. The vote 
will instead count as a vote for John Doe on the 
Party A ballot only. This provides the voter the 
opportunity to express their support for the 
candidate. 
Voters with party affiliations may change their party 
affiliation or become undeclared by completing a 
party change form at the clerk’s office or at a 
session of the supervisors of the checklist after 
election day. 
Confidential Voters 
A voter is entitled to be a confidential voter by 
presenting a valid protective order pursuant to 
RSA 173-B:4, or evidence the voter is a participant 
in the address confidentiality program established 
by RSA 7:46. The voter must make a request to 
the clerk or supervisors. The supervisors, using 
SVRS, mark the public checklist with an entry 
“Confidential Voter ” followed by a sequential 
number, i.e. 1 for the first such voter, 2 for the 
second, etc. The supervisors must then maintain a 
separate, confidential checklist of these voters. Do 
not disclose the confidential checklist to anyone 
other than the clerk and the moderator, except as 
otherwise provided by law. SVRS has provisions 
for marking voters confidential. Use SVRS to print 
the confidential checklist. 
Clerks must send any qualified confidential voter 
an absentee ballot. RSA 7:46 specifically provides 
that “program participant[s] shall automatically 
receive absentee ballots for all elections in the 
jurisdiction for which that individual is domiciled in 
the same manner as absentee voters pursuant to 
RSA 657:15.” 
If a voter or a person in the household of the voter 
is a victim of certain crimes and does not wish to 
have his or her name or address appear on the 
checklist, he or she may apply to participate in a 
confidentiality program through the Attorney 
General's Office. RSA 7:46. 
If a person appears at the polling place to register 
and vote in person and identifies himself or herself 
as either being protected by a court order issued 
under RSA 173 -B:4 or as a participant in the 
Attorney General’s address confidentiality 
program, under RSA 7:46, the supervisors and the 
moderator should provide the voter an opportunity 
to register and vote confidentially. The moderator 
must arrange for the voter to obtain a ballot without 
the voter’s name being publicly announced and 
the entry of the voter on the marked checklist used 
on election day must be as “Confidential Voter #.”  
Fill in “1” unless there are other confidential voters 
on the checklist, then use the next number in 
sequence. 
It is appropriate to ensure the voter knows that he 
or she may vote absentee at future elections and 
to encourage the voter to consult with the Attorney 
General’s Victim Witness Assistance Office 
regarding how to vote while remaining safe. RSA 
654:25; RSA 659:50. 
More information on the address confidentiality 
program may be obtained by contacting the 
Attorney General 's Office of Victim/Witness 
Assistance at 1-800-300-4500 or (603) 271-1240.

Declaration of Candidacy: The Secretary of State 
will provide each town and city clerk with a supply 
of Declaration of Candidacy forms. A person 
declaring candidacy will have their name printed 
on the official primary ballot of the party in which 
they are registered. The person signing the 
declaration of candidacy must be a registered 
voter in the town or ward where they file and must 
also be registered as a member of the party for 
which they are filing. It is the clerk’s 
responsibility to check SVRS and ensure those 
requirements are satisfied. At the time the 
candidate files their declaration, they must also 
pay the appropriate fee or submit sufficient primary 
petitions. See RSA 655:19-c. 
Official with Whom to File (RSA 655:15): 
1. For the offices of governor, United States 
senator, representative in Congress, 
councilor, state senator and county office, the 
candidate must file with the Secretary of 
State. 
2. For state representative in a representative 
district containing one town or ward and for 
delegate to a state party convention, the 
candidate may file with the secretary of state 
or with the clerk of the town or city in which 
the officer is to be chosen. 
3. For state representative in a representative 
district containing more than one town or 
ward, the candidate may file with the 
Secretary of State or with the clerk of the city 
or town in which the filer is domiciled (if the 
candidate is domiciled in an unincorporated 
place, they may also file with the town clerk of 
the town designated by the Secretary of State 
for such filing). 
Candidates for state representative must complete 
each portion of the declaration of candidacy form, 
including the affidavit of qualification and financial 
disclosure. RSA 655:14, 15, & 17. By filing for state 
representative, candidates also acknowledge that, 
if elected, they will serve as a delegate to the 
county convention (a member of the county 
legislative body). RSA 655:29. 
In order to file for state representative candidacy, 
the candidate must meet the following statutory 
and constitutional qualifications: “To hold the office 
of state representative, a person must be at least 
18 years of age and must be qualified as provided 
in Part 2, Article 14 of the state constitution: for 2 
years, at least, next preceding the election shall 
have been an inhabitant of the town, ward, place, 
or district he or she may be chosen to represent, 
and shall cease to represent such town, ward, 
place, or district immediately on his or her ceasing 
to be qualified as aforesaid.” RSA 655:8. 
Financial Interest Statement : RSA Chapter 15- A 
requires all candidates for state and county offices 
to file a statement of financial interest. The 
reporting form requires the candidates to identify 
professions, businesses, or organizations which 
were the source of more than $10,000 of income 
during the preceding calendar year. It also requires 
identifying broad categories of business and public 
policy where the candidate or their family member 
has a special interest. RSA 15-A:5. 
Delegate to the Republican State Convention: 
Delegates to the Republican State Convention are 
elected at the state primary election. The number 
of delegates to be elected mirrors the number of 
state representatives to be elected in the same 
district. RSA 662:6. Although candidates for 
delegate must file a Declaration of Candidacy 
form, candidates are not required to pay any fee or 
file any petitions. RSA 653:6. 
Candidates for Republican State Convention 
Delegate must be registered members of the 
Republican Party and must be domiciled in the 
town or city they are seeking to represent. 
The Democratic Party does not elect delegates; 
those who wish to attend the Democratic State 
Convention should contact the Democratic State 
Committee. 
Primary Petitions: A candidate seeking the 
nomination of a party may use a primary petition in 
lieu of paying a filing fee. Each primary petition 
may contain the name of only one candidate and

bear the signature of only one voter. In completing 
a primary petition, a voter’s oath is sufficient 
evidence that they are a member of the party 
stated. 
Voters shall not sign conflicting party petitions, nor 
shall they sign more than one primary petition for 
an office with only one available nomination. For 
example, a voter may sign up to eight primary 
petitions for a state representative race where 
eight candidates will be elected for that district. But 
that voter shall not sign more than one primary 
petition when only one candidate will be elected to 
that position. If a voter has signed two or more 
conflicting primary petitions, all petitions from that 
voter shall be rejected. RSA 655:21, 23, 24. 
An Assent to Candidacy/Declaration of Candidacy 
form completed by the candidate must accompany 
any primary petition filed. The candidate must 
complete every portion of the form, including the 
affidavit of qualification and the financial 
disclosure. RSA 655:25; RSA 15-A:3. 
It is the duty of the clerk with whom the petitions 
are filed to examine them. If a petition conflicts with 
the law, the clerk shall mark on the petition the 
reason it was rejected and return the petition within 
24 hours to the candidate. For each rejected 
petition, the candidate may file a supplementary 
petition with the clerk no later than the last day of 
the filing period for declarations of candidacy. RSA 
655:26. 
Party Committee Nominations: If no declarations 
of candidacy or primary petitions are filed on behalf 
of a candidate for any office, the chairperson of the 
appropriate party committee or their designee may 
make a nomination to fill the vacancy by notifying 
the Secretary of State within 10 business days 
following the close of the filing period. 
Party committee nominations made in this manner 
are responsible to pay the appropriate fee or 
submit the requisite number of petitions. An 
affidavit of qualifications must accompany the 
name of the nominated candidates within the time 
limit. RSA 655:29. 
Mail Completed Forms: Declarations of candidacy, 
primary petitions, assents to candidacy, and RSA 
15-A statements of financial interest must be 
mailed by the town or city clerk to the 
Secretary of State on the same day they are 
filed. 
Clerks must also send a daily electronic summary 
of all filings received on that day. Summaries must 
include the name and address of every candidate 
who filed. Reports are only required to be filed on 
days the clerks’ offices are open and receiving 
filings. A fillable PDF form for making these daily 
reports is available in SVRS Help Instructions . 
Complete the form, save a copy locally, and attach 
the form in an email to elections@sos.nh.gov. RSA 
655:18, 27. 
All candidates filing on the last day of the filing 
period must do so in person. Clerk offices must be 
open from, at least, 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on the 
last day of the filing period. Candidates for all other 
offices must file with the Secretary of State . RSA 
652:20; RSA 655:15-16. 
F
OR GENERAL ELECTION 
Candidates who choose not to run as a Democrat 
or Republican may have their name placed on the 
state general election ballot by filing a declaration 
of intent along with an administrative assessment 
fee (set by RSA 655:19 -c) with the Secretary of 
State during the regular primary filing period. The 
candidate is required to later file the requisite 
number of nomination papers. RSA 655:14-a, 17-
a, 19-c, 40, & 45. Filings made on the final day of 
the primary filing period must be done so in person 
before the Secretary of State. RSA 655:43, II. 
Only registered voters may sign nomination 
papers. Each voter may only sign one nomination 
paper for each office, and each nomination paper 
shall not contain the names of more candidates 
than there are offices to be filled. Voters shall sign 
and date an individual nomination paper; note that 
nomination papers shall be dated in the year of the 
election.

Submit Nomination Paper s to Supervisors for 
Certification: Completed nomination papers shall 
be submitted to the Supervisors of the Checklist no 
later than 5:00 p.m. on the Wednesday five weeks 
prior to the State Primary Election (beginning in 
2028, this will be the Friday five weeks prior to the 
State Primary Election). 
Nomination papers include a section completed by 
the supervisors. The supervisors sign the 
nomination paper in the provided space after 
confirming that the individual who signed the 
nomination paper is a voter in their community. A 
majority of the supervis ors must certify and sign 
the nomination papers. In a city, the city clerk may 
certify the nomination papers (and be the sole 
signer) instead of the registrars. 
Certified nomination papers must be available for 
the candidate no later than 5:00 p.m. on the 
Wednesday (or, in 2028, the Friday) two weeks 
prior to the primary, and the candidate must submit 
the nomination papers to the Secretary of State no 
later than 5:00 p.m. on the Wednesday (or, in 
2028, the Friday) one week prior to the primary. 
Nomination papers shall be grouped by 
municipality when submitted, or the Secretary of 
State may reject them. RSA 655:41-43. 
Party Ticket Vacancies: If a vacancy in any party 
ticket occurs after a primary, the appropriate party 
committee may appoint someone to fill the 
vacancy, provided they do so within three days of 
the notice of disqualification or death and further 
provided that the name of the substitute candidate 
is received by the Secretary of State no later than 
the Tuesday prior to the election. RSA 655:38; 
RSA 655:39. 
Incompatible Offices 
State & County Incompatible Offices : Candidates 
filing for the state primary may not file for more 
than one of the following offices: governor, U.S. 
senator, U.S. representative, executive councilor, 
state senator, state representative, county 
commissioner, county sheriff, county attorney, 
county treasurer, register of deeds, and register or 
probate. No person shall seek or hold positions as 
a member of the general court and county 
commissioner at the same time. RSA 655:10. 
Local Incompatible Offices : RSA 669:7 sets forth 
several statutorily incompatible local offices.  No 
person may hold two incompatible local offices at 
the same time. RSA 669:7, I. No person may file 
a declaration of candidacy for two or more elected 
offices that are incompatible. RSA 669:7, II. 
C
ANDIDATE DISQUALIFICATION OR DEATH BEFORE 
PRIMARY 
If any candidate dies or becomes disqualified 
between the close of the filing period and the date 
of the primary, the Secretary of State may remove 
their name from the ballot, and the appropriate 
party committee may substitute a new candidate. 
RSA 655:33-34. 
Candidate disqualification is limited by statute; a 
candidate may only disqualify themselves by 
making an oath that they do not qualify for the 
public office which they seek because age, 
domicile, or incapacitating physical or mental 
disability acquired subsequent to the nomination 
or filing. RSA 655:33, 38. 
Domicile Concerns: Elected or appointed officials 
whose qualifications for that position require 
specific domicile are considered to have resigned 
if they move their domicile in a way which no 
longer qualifies them to be a voter in the area they 
represented or served. Any vacancy created shall 
be filled as prescribed by law. RSA 654:1, II. 
Administrative Preparations 
CLERK CONTACT AND POLLING PLACE 
INFORMATION 
Each town and city clerk shall establish and 
maintain an up- to-date official e -mail address, 
street address, up -to-date polling place 
location(s), and polling hours for each election, all 
of which shall be entered into SVRS and publicly 
available to voters. RSA 657:19-c.

OATHS OF OFFICE 
Inspectors of elections (ballot clerks), appointed 
assistant election officials, moderators pro tem, 
supervisors pro tem, clerks pro tem, and 
selectmen pro tem, including anyone recruited to 
count ballots, all must take an oath of office before 
engaging in the duties of their position. 
Blank Oath of Office forms are available in SVRS 
Help Instructions . The wording of the Oath of 
Office is set by the New Hampshire Constitution, 
Part 2, Article 84. Officials administering an oath 
must file the completed Oath of Office forms with 
the clerk. RSA 42:1, 7 -8; RSA 658:4. The clerk 
shall retain the completed Oa th of Office form for 
the term of the office plus 3 years. RSA 33- A:3-a, 
XCI. 
P
RINTING OF ELECTION MATERIALS 
The Secretary of State prepares ballots, forms, 
and absentee voter materials for all state elections 
and state referenda, including constitutional 
amendments. RSA 656:1. 
Regular and Sample Ballots: Ballots for state 
elections are delivered to town and city clerks prior 
to the election. 
State and Presidential Primary Sample Ballots: 
The package of primary election ballots will include 
10 sample ballots for each political party. Clerk s 
shall post two sets of sample ballots in public 
places in the town or ward within one day after they 
receive them. The remainder of the sample ballots 
are posted on election day outside the guardrail in 
the polling place. RSA 656:28. 
General Sample Ballots: 10 sample ballots are 
printed and sent to the town or ward clerk. Post a 
sample ballot in two public places within the 
community within one day after receiving them. 
The remainder of the sample ballots are to be 
posted outside the guardrail in the polling area on 
election day. RSA 656:18. 
At least one sample ballot from each party in a 
primary, and one sample ballot in a general 
election shall be posted by the clerk no higher than 
48” to ensure the posted sample ballots are 
accessible for all. RSA 658:26. 
Absentee Ballots: Absentee ballots and Federal 
Office Only (“FOO”) absentee ballots are also 
prepared by the Secretary of State . As soon as 
they are available, they are delivered to the clerks 
along with envelopes, instructions, and application 
forms. RSA 656:33-38. 
Registration Forms & Election Day Affidavits: The 
supervisors of the checklist shall ensure that a 
sufficient quantity of voter registration forms are 
available at the polling place for election day 
registration of all qualified persons at all elections. 
P
OLLING LOCATION MATERIALS 
Notice of Voter Photo Identification Requirements: 
Every town and city clerk, and the governing body 
of each town or ward, shall prominently display a 
notice prepared by the Secretary of State 
explaining the photo identification requirements for 
voters. The notice directs voters to the Department 
of State’s website for additional information. 
Display the notice for at least 14 days prior to each 
election. RSA 652:25; RSA 658:29- a. This notice 
is also placed outside the guardrail at each polling 
place at all elections. 
Mandatory Voter Instruction Signs : Moderators 
must ensure that all mandatory voter instruction 
signs – also known as Purity of Election Posters – 
are posted in each polling place. Each sign is 
labeled with its version on the bottom edge. Some 
mandatory voter instruction signs are tailored to 
specific election conditions. For example, some 
signs are exclusive to a hand- count town for a 
primary election. The following chart indicates the 
name of each sign and the approved version.

CERTIFICATION OF THE CHECKLIST 
The checklist(s) used at the election must be 
certified at two different moments in time by two 
different sets of officials. Before the election, the 
supervisors must certify that the corrected 
checklist, according to their best knowledge, 
contains (fill in number) of names of those persons 
“who are by actual domicile legal voters” in the 
town or ward. RSA 654:29. Two certified copies 
must be provided to the clerk. Election officials in 
hand count towns must use both certified copies 
as the checklist for the election; election officials in 
machine count towns must use one certified copy 
as the checklist for the election. 
After the polls close to voting, the moderator and 
the clerk must certify the checklist marked by the 
ballot clerks, under the supervision of the 
moderator, throughout election day and on which 
the names of those who registered on election day 
have been entered. The moderator and clerk 
certify that it is the checklist used by them on 
election day and that it contains a correct and 
complete list of the legal voters in their town or 
ward, including those who registered on election 
day. RSA 659:56. 
P
OSTING OF WARRANT FOR GENERAL ELECTIONS 
The town and ward selectmen are responsible for 
warning the time and date for general elections. 
The warrant must state the hour when the polls 
will open to voting and the hour before which the 
polls may not close. The warrant must also list 
the offices to be elected, questions to be voted on 
by ballot, and the polling place location. RSA 
658:1; 669:2. Note: in cities, although ward 
selectmen are responsible for posting polling 
hours, the city council or board of aldermen sets 
the polling hours. 
The warrant must be posted at least 14 days prior 
to any election at all polling places and at the office 
of the town or city clerk or at the town hall. See 
deadline dates in the New Hampshire Political 
Calendar published by the Secretary of State, and 
currently available online: 
https://www.sos.nh.gov/elections/2026-2027-
political-calendar. 
Polling Place Preparation 
For all presidential primary, state primary, and 
general elections, the Secretary of State’s Office 
prepares ballots and delivers them to town and city 
clerks prior to each election. 
Inspect Ballots Upon Receipt : The town or city 
clerk must open all boxes of ballots received from 
the Secretary of State for a state election in the 
presence of at least one other voter as soon as 
possible after those boxes are received. The clerk 
must verify that all ballots are the proper ones for 
that town or city, remove the number of ballots 
needed to test the electronic ballot counting device 
(if applicable) and the Accessible Voting System , 
and then reseal the boxes using the sealing label 
provided in the box. RSA 656:20, 22, & 29.
