Ballot Inventory: Election officials must conduct a 
ballot inventory at or prior to the opening of the 
polls in each polling place. Conducting a ballot 
inventory prior to polls opening helps prevent 
delays or other issues on election day morning. If 
the ballots are counted prior to the opening of the 
polls, the clerk shall post in two appropriate places 
a notice detailing the time and place where the 
ballots will be publicly counted. 
At or prior to the opening of the polls in each polling 
location, the ballot box seal shall be publicly 
broken by the town or ward clerk. The ballots shall 
be given to the ballot clerks, who examine and 
count the ballots in the presence of the clerk, the 
moderator, and at least one other legal voter. Note 
that candidates on the ballot – except those 
candidates who serve as a moderator, assistant 
moderator, clerk, selectperson, inspector of 
election, or supervisor of the checklist – shall not 
count ballots. RSA 658:31. 
Pre-Election Certificate : The Secretary of State 
prepares and distributes three copies of the Pre -
Election Certificate required by RSA 658:32 to 
each clerk for all state elections. After completing 
ballot inventory, the moderator and clerk shall 
certify in Part I of the Pre -Election Certificate the 
total number of official ballots received. One copy 
is retained by the moderator for their records; one 
copy is retained by the clerk for their records; and 
one copy is forwarded to the Secretary of State 
with the election returns. RSA 658:32; see RSA 
659:75. 
B
ALLOT COUNTING DEVICES 
The mayor and aldermen of a city or the selectmen 
of a town may elect to use electronic ballot 
counting devices in their communities. RSA 
656:40. 
Adoption: RSA 656:40 authorizes the governing 
body of a town or city to approve one of the 
electronic ballot counting devices certified by the 
Ballot Law Commission. This decision must be 
made in a properly noticed public meeting; for 
example, this can be a regularly scheduled and 
noticed meeting of the Board of Selectmen where 
this item is on the agenda and the discussion and 
vote is properly documented in the minutes. The 
vote needs to be specific as to the device that will 
be used. 
The municipality must send formal notice to the 
Secretary of State reporting what device will be 
used in the future. This can be a letter signed by 
the Selectboard. Alternatively, this can be a letter 
from the Administrator or Clerk that attaches the 
approved minutes of the meeting where the vote 
was taken. 
Device Testing: The clerk is responsible for testing 
all electronic ballot counting devices and 
programmed external storage devices in the 
municipality’s possession. RSA 656:42, 
VIII(e)(10). Testing must be conducted during a 
publicly noticed meeting no later than the 
Wednesday before an election. Specific testing 
standards and guidance is available in SVRS Help 
Instructions.  
Clerks must ensure that the pre-election testing is 
documented by preserving the test ballots, the 
count of votes on the test ballots made by the town 
or city clerk, and the results from the electronic 
ballot counting device that was testing. 
Documentation of the pre-election testing must be 
readily available on election day. Note that the pre-
election certificate requires the moderator and the 
clerk to and certify  on election day that there is 
evidence of successful pre- election testing on 
each electronic ballot counting device and each 
memory device in the town or city clerk’s 
possession. 
Clerks and moderators are additionally required to 
certify, by signature on the pre-election certification 
on election day, that all electronic ballot counting 
device seals are present, all seals have been 
maintained intact, and that any seals which have 
been broken were appropriately resealed and 
documented in the activity log. 
Activity Logs: Each ballot counting device must be 
sealed in the manner required by the Secretary of

State. Activity logs are available in SVRS Help 
Instructions. Seals ensure that a ballot counting 
device cannot be tampered with or improperly 
accessed. An activity log for each ballot counting 
device is available on SVRS. The activity log 
documents each removal and installation of seals 
on a ballot counting device, and specifically 
requires the date, which seal was installed or 
removed, the number imprinted on that seal, the 
reason for the removal or installation, a signature 
by the remover or installer, and signatures from 
two witnesses. 
The activity log provides a history of each time an 
individual accessed the device; missing entries – 
for example, a seal placed on a device with no 
matching entry – may be due to a forgotten log 
entry, but it can also be a possible indicator of 
improper or unauthorized access to the device. 
Election officials should contact the Secretary of 
State’s Office for guidance regarding all missing 
log entries. 
A
CCESSIBLE VOTING SYSTEM 
New Hampshire law requires each polling place be 
equipped with at least one accessible voting 
system (“AVS”) for every election. RSA 659:20 -b. 
The Secretary of State chose the OmniBallot 
Tablet to replace the “One4All” device and provide 
accessible voting for individuals with disabilities. 
The OmniBallot Tablet prints a voter’s choices 
directly on to an official ballot, and that ballot is cast 
in the same manner as all other ballots in that 
polling place. 
The OmniBallot Tablet utilizes several types of 
accessible options, including magnification, 
compatibility with assistive technology, 
headphones, and tactile buttons, to ensure voters 
with disabilities can mark their ballots 
independently and privately. Although the 
OmniBallot Tablet has features which specifically 
aim to provide greater accessibility to voters with 
disabilities, the OmniBallot Tablet is available 
for use by all voters in all elections. Election 
officials should not request a voter disclose their 
disability, and voters are not required to disclose 
their disability in order to use the OmniBallot 
Tablet. Any voter may use the OmniBallot, 
regardless of disability status, upon request. 
Information related to the security and storage 
guidelines, setting up the AVS, and programming 
guidance is available in SVRS Help Instructions . 
The OmniBallot Tablet must also be tested prior to 
each election. 
A
DOPTING ADDITIONAL POLLING PLACES 
Any town may vote at the town meeting to provide 
additional polling places and to establish the 
districts to be served by them. The selectmen of 
the town are responsible for equipping the 
additional polling place in the same manner as the 
central polling place. The moderator must appoint 
an assistant moderator, and the clerk must appoint 
an assistant clerk for each additional polling place. 
Current law requires assistant moderators and 
clerks appointed in towns to be domiciled in that 
town, but not necessarily the voting district, of the 
additional polling place. RSA 658:10, 14, 15, 16. 
The city council in any city may establish additional 
voting districts within the wards of the city. The city 
council is responsible for designating the districts 
within the wards and selecting the various election 
officials to run the polling place unless the city 
charter provides otherwise. In the same manner as 
towns, the moderator must appoint an assistant 
moderator, and the clerk must appoint an assistant 
clerk for each additional polling place; each 
assistant moderator and assistant clerk shall have 
their domicile in the city ward where they will serve. 
RSA 658:10, 11, 14, & 18. 
Two additional inspectors of election for each 
additional polling place are to be designated by 
each political party. The inspectors must be 
domiciled in the town and qualified in the same 
manner as the officers of the central polling place. 
RSA 658:14-15. 
Supervisors must prepare a list of the voters 
entitled to vote in the polling place using SVRS. No

post a copy at the town or city clerk’s office or at

All officers of the additional polling place shall have

together and establish a written continuity of

common emergencies and effective local 
responses. A model COOP is available in the

by absentee ballot on the day immediately 
prior to the election. 
The authorization to vote absentee when the 
National Weather Service has issued a severe 
weather warning applies where the voter would 
have voted in person but has concerns for their 
safety if they travel in the storm, or where the voter 
anticipates that school, child care, or adult care will 
be cancelled and the voter would be deterred from 
voting by the need to care for children or infirm 
adults. RSA 657:1. 
The clerk’s office is required to be open to receive 
applications for absentee ballots, to allow voters to 
complete the absentee ballots, and to receive 
return ballots from at least 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. 
on the Monday immediately prior to an election. 
RSA 652:20; 654:7, 12; 657:1. 
P
UBLIC HEALTH CONSIDERATIONS AND ABSENTEE 
VOTING 
A voter would qualify to vote by absentee ballot 
and register by absentee registration if the voter, 
based on their personal judgment and individual 
medical circumstances of the voter, is advised by 
medical authorities to avoid going out in public. 
This applies to a voter experiencing symptoms of 
any communicable disease or illness. It would also 
apply to a voter limited public exposure as a 
preventative measure due to medical 
circumstances where voting or registering by 
absentee registration would be consistent with that 
voter’s general, preventative measures behaviors. 
These voters have a reasonable basis to conclude 
that a “physical disability” exists within the 
meaning of RSA 654:16-17. 
Applying for an Absentee Ballot 
Voters eligible to vote absentee must apply to the 
clerk in the town or city in which they are domiciled 
using a form provided by the Secretary of State on 
its website 
(https://www.sos.nh.gov/elections/absentee-
ballots). The application requires the voter provide 
their phone number and email address. However, 
some voters may not possess or may opt not to 
provide this information, treat the application as 
valid if this information is missing. The phone 
number and email address provided are 
confidential and exempt from disclosure under the 
Right-to-Know law. RSA 654:31-a. 
The law now requires an identity verification for 
non-UOCAVA absentee ballot applications. RSA 
657:17-c. Absentee ballots cannot be issued 
unless an applicant provides sufficient verification 
with one of the three following identity verification 
methods: 
1. Provide a copy of the voter’s photo 
identification that meets the requirements of 
RSA 659:13, II(a); 
2. Personally present a photo identification to 
the clerk or their designee which meets the 
requirements of RSA 659:13, II(a); or 
3. Notarize the voter’s signature on their 
absentee ballot application. 
Non-UOCAVA absentee ballots cannot be mailed 
or issued unless the clerk has received an 
application along with photo identification or a 
notarized signature as detailed above. If a clerk 
receives an informal request – for example: an 
emailed request for an absentee ballot without an 
application – the clerk should send the voter an 
absentee ballot application or direct them to the 
form available on the Secretary of State’s website. 
The absentee ballot application and one of the 
three sufficient verification methods can be sent by 
e-mail, mail, fax, or delivered in person to town and 
city clerks. 
All non -UOCAVA voters must submit a separate 
absentee ballot application for the primary election 
and the general election. 
Non-UOCAVA absentee ballot applications must 
be postmarked or received within six months of the 
election for which the absentee ballot is requested. 
RSA 657:6. Applications received more than six 
months before the election for which the absentee 
ballot was requested must be rejected, and the 
clerk shall notify the applicant within seven days

V
OTERS WITH PRINT DISABILITIES 
New Hampshire provides an opportunity for 
individuals with print disabilities to electronically 
receive and mark their absentee ballot for any 
state election. An accessible electronic absentee 
ballot application is available to download on the 
Secretary of State’s website: 
https://www.sos.nh.gov/elections/voting-
disabilities. 
Voters with print disabilities must send the form to 
their town or city clerk and call the Secretary of 
State’s Election Division (603-271-8241) to inform 
them that an application to use the electronic 
system was submitted. 
UOCAVA V
OTERS 
The absentee ballot process differs for UOCAVA 
voters. UOCAVA – the Uniformed and Overseas 
Citizens Absentee Voting Act – is a federal law 
which prescribes forms and processes for voter 
registration, requests for absentee ballots, and 
absentee ballot delivery deadlines. UOCAVA 
voters include all active-service military branches, 
their dependents, and overseas U.S. citi zen 
voters. 
UOCAVA voters can request an absentee ballot 
using a Federal Post Card Application (“FPCA”) 
form from their local town or city clerk, or by 
downloading an application on www.fvap.gov. The 
federal official post card forms for UOCAVA voters 
shall be received no earlier than January of the 
calendar year in which the election occurs. FPCA 
requests received on or after January 1 of each 
year are valid through December 31 of the same 
year for all state and municipal elections to be held 
within that year, subject to the UOCAVA voter’s 
request and eligibility. However, an absentee ballot 
for a presidential primary shall be sent to any 
UOCAVA voters who submitted an application for 
the presidential primary or any election prior to the 
primary during the general election year and the 
prior year. RSA 657:19-a. 
Receipt of Absentee Ballot Application
by Clerk 
Absentee ballot applications may be received in 
person or by mail, e-mail, or fax. Upon receipt, the 
clerk shall determine if the applicant’s name is on 
the checklist, the application is signed by the 
applicant, the applicant marked their qualifying 
circumstance which permits absentee voting in the 
appropriate place, and one of the three identity 
verification methods is satisfied. 
If the a bsentee applicant is not registered or 
pending registration approval in that town, the 
clerk shall mark the absentee ballot application 
“Not Registered” and send the applicant: (a) an 
absentee registration form; (b) absentee ballot, if 
available; (c) affidavit envelope, marked with 
words “Not Registered;” (d) return envelope, 
marked with the words “Not Registered;” (e) notice 
of requirements for absentee voting; and (f) written 
notice of what documents and forms the applicant 
must return in order for their absentee ballot to be 
counted. 
On receipt of a request for an accessible electronic 
absentee ballot, the clerk will scan the application 
and send it to NHVotes@sos.nh.gov and call the 
Elections Division Help Desk (603 -271-8241) to 
verify that it has been received. The Secretary of 
State will copy the clerk on the email message to 
the voter. The clerk will mail out the absentee ballot 
envelopes and instructions to the voter. When the 
clerk receives the mailing envelope expected to 
contain a voter’s marked absentee ballot and 
absentee affidavit, it must be entered in SVRS in 
the same manner as all absentee ballots. 
L
IST OF ABSENTEE VOTERS MAINTAINED BY CLERK 
The clerk shall maintain a list by date, arranged by 
voting place, of all absentee applicants (regular 
and UOCAVA) who (a) have requested an 
absentee ballot, (b) have been sent an absentee

suspected to contain absentee ballots. This

essential to allow a voter to track the progress of 
their absentee ballot on the Secretary of State ’s 
“Voter Information Lookup” website, available 
here: https://app.sos.nh.gov/viphome. RSA 
657:15, 26. 
C
ANDIDATE ABSENTEE BALLOT LIST 
Clerks are required to provide the list of persons 
requesting absentee ballots to a candidate whose 
name appears on the ballot for the ward/district 
they are a candidate for. The information provided 
must be limited to the voter’s name, address where 
registered, voter ID number, voter’s party, the type 
of election the absentee ballot was requested for, 
the date the absentee ballot was requested, the 
date the absentee ballot was sent or handed to the 
voter, and the date the absentee ballot envelope 
was returned. The law requires that if a candidate, 
whose name appears on the ballot, requests the 
list in electronic format, it must be provided free of 
charge. RSA 657:15, II. 
The list of persons requesting absentee ballots is 
not a public document and clerks may only provide 
it to a candidate whose name appears on the ballot 
or their designee for the ward district they are a 
candidate for. If a designee presents the request, 
the designee must have a notarized request 
signed by the candidate (or a copy of said 
notarized request). Once the election is held, that 
person is no longer a candidate, and they (and 
their designee) are no longer eligible to obtain a 
copy. RSA 657:15. 
Candidates whose names appear on the ballot for 
statewide office may obtain a list of absentee voter 
applicants from the Secretary of State. Political 
parties may also obtain a statewide list of absentee 
voter applicants from the Secretary of State. 
Statewide absentee voter lists are limited to the 
voter’s name and address where registered, voter 
ID number, voter’s party, the type of election the 
absentee ballots were requested for, the date the 
absentee ballot was requested, the date the 
absentee ballot was sent or handed to the voter, 
and the date the absentee ballot envelope was 
returned. The statewide list must be provided at 
least once per week and at least twice each week 
for the four weeks prior to the election. RSA 
657:15, III-a, IV. 
The list of absentee voter applicants shall not be 
available for public inspection at any time without 
a court order. The list excludes confidential voters 
who have presented to the supervisors of the 
checklist valid protective orders pursuant to RSA 
173-B:4 or who are participants in the Attorney 
General’s Address Confidentiality program. RSA 
7:43; RSA 657:15. 
People interested in information on who voted 
absentee are, after the election, entitled to see 
and/or copy the checklist used on election day, 
where absentee voters are marked with a red ink 
“A.V.”, the voter is checked off, and a single thin 
line is drawn through the last name to mark the 
voter as having voted. 
At the polling place on election day for all rejected 
absentee ballots, the moderator shall record next 
to the name of the absentee voter on the clerk’s list 
the word “rejected” and the reason for the 
rejection. Do NOT record the rejection on the 
official checklist. A list of the permitted absentee 
ballot rejection reasons can be found in SVRS 
Help Instructions. 
Sending Absentee Ballots 
CLERKS TO SEND OR DELIVER ABSENTEE BALLOTS 
The clerk must mail or personally deliver the 
absentee ballot, making certain that the 
appropriate ballot, affidavit, and instructions are 
enclosed, without delay. If the application for an 
absentee ballot does not state that the voter will be 
absent from town or unable to vote in person due 
to religious observance, physical disability, or work 
obligations, the clerk should also send a notice of 
the requirements for absentee voting.

The clerk may designate an assistant to deliver an 
absentee ballot, provided that the assistant is not 
a candidate for office or working for a candidate. 
The clerk shall mail absentee ballots in response 
to verified absentee ballot requests that have been 
received by 12:00 p.m. on the day before the 
election. The clerk shall provide an absentee ballot 
to any voter requesting an absentee ballot in 
person at the clerk’s office up until 5:00 p.m. on the 
day before the election. RSA 657:15. If the clerk’s 
office is open later than 5:00 p.m., it is permissible 
to issue an over -the-counter absentee ballot until 
the clerk’s office closes; 5:00 p.m. is a minimum 
requirement, not a deadline. 
S
ENDING ABSENTEE BALLOTS TO UOCAVA 
VOTERS 
Upon receipt of a properly executed application for 
an absentee ballot from a UOCAVA voter, a town 
or city clerk shall retain the application and, without 
delay, enter the application into SVRS . RSA 
657:10-b, 19, 26. 
The clerk shall send the appropriate ballot and 
materials without delay, regardless of whether the 
applicant appears on the checklist. Absentee 
ballots for UOCAVA voters can be sent by mail or 
email, as requested by the voter. RSA 657:19. 
Note: if a UOCAVA voter does not indicate a party 
affiliation, they cannot vote in a primary election. If 
a UOCAVA voter is undeclared, requested an 
absentee ballot for a primary, and did not identify 
which party’s ballot they are requesting, clerks are 
encouraged to reach out to the UOCAVA voter to 
identify the party with which they seek to affiliate. 
Clerks must send the Return to Undeclared Form 
to any undeclared absentee voter who requests to 
vote a party primary ballot. Political party affiliation 
is not required to vote in a general election. 
A
BSENTEE BALLOTS FOR EMERGENCY SERVICE 
WORKERS 
If an emergency services worker receives notice 
after noon on the Friday before an election that 
they are being called into service under 
circumstances that will prevent that person from 
voting in person or by absentee using the usual 
procedures, the Secretary of State’s office should 
be informed. The Secretary of State, with 
assistance from the Attorney General and the 
Department of Safety, will make every reasonable 
effort to get absentee ballots and materials to 
these emergency service workers and back to the 
local polling places. 
This law waives the usual requirement that ballots 
be received at the polls by 5:00 p.m. Under this 
law, any absentee ballot received before the polls 
close from a deployed emergency services worker, 
if found properly qualified, must be counted. 
Local election officials should make an effort to 
ensure that local emergency services workers are 
aware of this law. In the event of a local emergency 
that ties up local emergency services workers and 
prevents those who planned to vote in person at 
the polls from doing so, local officials should 
contact the Secretary of State and make 
arrangements for a local official to transport 
absentee ballots and materials to the site of the 
local emergency and afford qualified emergency 
services the opportunity to cast absentee ballots. 
RSA 657:21-a. 
V
OTER TRACKING OF ABSENTEE BALLOT 
The clerk should provide instructions to absentee 
voter applicants describing how to access the 
Secretary of State’s website to determine whether: 
• 
• 
• 
• 
Their absentee ballot request was 
received; 
The clerk has sent the absentee ballot to 
the voter; 
Their returned ballot was received by the 
clerk; and 
The absentee ballot was counted or 
rejected by the moderator (and, if rejected, 
the reason for rejection). 
Voters can determine the status of their absentee 
ballot at https://app.sos.nh.gov/viphome.

INCARCERATED PERSONS 
A person incarcerated because of a felony 
conviction is not eligible to register or vote while 
incarcerated. RSA 607- A:2. A voter who is 
incarcerated for a misdemeanor or who is held in 
a penal institution while awaiting trial, however, 
does have the right to vote by absentee ballot. 
RSA 657:4, 7. When completing a voter 
registration form an absentee ballot application, an 
incarcerated person must list the address of their 
domicile prior to incarceration in the address 
section and the address of the penal institution in 
the mailing address section. RSA 654:2-a. 
Returning Absentee Ballots 
A voter who has received an official absentee 
ballot must either mail, personally deliver, or have 
a delivery agent deliver it to the city or town clerk. 
RSA 657:17. 
Town and city clerks must be available for 
absentee voters to request or drop off a completed 
absentee ballot in its envelopes between 3 and 5 
p.m. on the day before any election. Note, 
however, that RSA 657:7 and 657:16 were 
amended: ALL absentee ballots must be sealed in 
the affidavit envelope (form A), but ONLY absentee 
ballots that are mailed to the clerk need to be 
sealed in the outer envelope. An absentee voter 
who hand delivers their absentee ballot properly 
sealed in affidavit envelope (form A) with all 
supporting documentation does not need to place 
these documents in the outer envelope. If they 
nevertheless hand deliver their documentation in 
the outer envelope, the clerk cannot open that 
outer envelope. If an absentee voter presents 
photo ID when hand delivering their absentee 
ballot, the clerk must mark voter verified on the 
affidavit envelope (or write “voter verified” on the 
outer envelope if the affidavit envelope is sealed in 
the outer envelope) and record this in SVRS. 
If a voter brings their absentee ballot in person to 
the polling place on election day, the voter must be 
instructed to vote in person using an election day 
ballot. The voter must turn in the absentee ballot, 
and election officials must reject that ballot, 
preserve it unopened, and mark "voted in person" 
on the unopened ballot. The rejection reason must 
be entered into SVRS. 
Absentee ballots delivered by mail shall be 
accepted no later than 5 p.m. on election day. RSA 
652:20; 657:22. 
A delivery agent may hand deliver an absentee 
ballot to the town or city clerk’s office or, on election 
day, to the town, city, or ward clerk at the polling 
place as late as 5:00 p.m. Only the following are 
authorized by law to serve as a delivery agent: 
•
 
• 
• 
• 
The v
oter’s spouse, parent, sibling, child, 
grandchild, father -in-law, mother-in-law, son-
in-law, daughter-in-law, stepparent, stepchild; 
The administrator or administrator’s designee 
of a nursing home, if the voter is a resident of 
the nursing home; 
The administrator or administrator’s designee 
of a residential care facility, if the voter is a 
resident of the residential care facility; or 
A person who assists a voter with a disability 
with voting absentee and signs their name on 
the affidavit on the line for identifying a person 
who assisted the voter. This type of delivery 
agent is limited to delivering no more than four 
absentee ballots in any election. 
RSA 657:17. A delivery agent must sign an 
Absentee Ballot Return Form when delivering an 
absentee ballot on election day. As a best practice, 
even prior to election day, clerks should request 
the delivery agents complete an Absentee Ballot 
Return Form when delivering absentee ballots to 
the clerk’s office. A completed form helps the clerk 
ensure the absentee ballot is received from a 
person authorized by law to make the delivery. 
R
ECEIPT OF MARKED ABSENTEE BALLOTS BY 
CLERK 
Upon receipt of an outer envelope or an affidavit 
envelope purporting to contain an absentee ballot, 
the clerk shall attach the voter’s application for an 
absentee ballot to the envelope submitted by said

The envelopes shall be preserved unopened until

Any absentee ballots received in the mail prior to

D
EATH OF AN ABSENTEE VOTER 
If the election officials counting ballots have 
knowledge that an absentee voter has died prior to 
the opening of the polls, do not open the absentee 
affidavit envelope and do not count the vote. RSA 
659:48. Consult with the Secretary of State’s 
Office regarding how to proceed. 
D
ETERMINING ABSENTEE BALLOT VOTER IDENTITY 
– HAND DELIVERY 
The amended law permits hand -delivered 
absentee ballots to be placed in just the affidavit 
envelope (form A) and does not require the outer 
envelope. Election officials should ensure they 
validate a voter’s information when an absentee 
ballot is hand- delivered prior to the voter leaving 
the office. 
If the voter’s information was not validated and the 
voter’s identity cannot be determined, check to see 
if the voter provided their address on the affidavit 
envelope. If they did, search SVRS by address, 
and then compare to the absentee ballot list to see 
if one of the applications is outstanding. 
If the voter did not provide their address, record the 
date the absentee ballot was received on the 
affidavit envelope. On election day, the moderator 
should determine which applications are still 
outstanding and try to match the signature of the 
voter with the affidavit versus the application. If the 
moderator is unable to determine which voter the 
affidavit was received from, the ballot should be 
rejected. 
Absentee Voters – Not Registered 
Upon receipt of an outer envelope marked “Not 
Registered,” the clerk shall open the outer 
envelope. If the applicant returns the required 
documents before the supervisors’ final session, it 
is best practice for the clerk to enter the applicant 
into SVRS in the “Pending” status, which allows 
the clerk to enter the voter and all the absentee 
ballot information in SVRS so it will appear on the 
absentee ballot list. The voter, however, cannot 
look up the status of their absentee ballot online 
until the Super visors meet and approve the 
application. Forward any voter registration 
documents to the supervisors of the checklist 
immediately upon receipt. 
If a voter registration application is received after 
the supervisors’ last session before the election, 
do NOT enter the voter into SVRS. The voter will 
be treated as an election day registration and all 
forms will need to go to the polls on election day. If 
the voter is entered prior to election day, the 
supervisors will not be able to accurately balance 
their checklist of election day voters because the 
voter registration date will not show as election 
day. 
If the supervisors find the applicant to be qualified, 
the applicant shall be added to the checklist and 
the absentee ballot shall be processed in the same 
manner as the absentee ballot of a previously 
registered voter. 
The town or city clerk shall notify the individuals 
with deficient or incomplete absentee ballot 
application documents of the deficiency within 
seven days of receipt of the application. RSA 
657:16. 
If the voter returns the absentee ballot without the 
required registration documents, the ballot, in its 
envelopes, shall be brought to the polling place, 
ruled on by the supervisors, marked, and 
preserved in the manner set forth by law for a

supervisors shall notify the moderator who shall 
reject the absentee ballot as “Not a registered 
voter.” RSA 657:16. 
The affidavit envelope (with its contents) of a 
successfully challenged absentee voter shall be 
preserved unopened, stored with the ballots, and 
destroyed unopened when the retention period for 
ballots expires. RSA 657:16. 
The supervisors shall write an adequate 
description of their decision on the Asserting a 
Challenge form or otherwise in the voter’s records. 
The clerk shall note the outcome of the challenge 
on the clerk’s absentee ballot list. RSA 654:7, 13; 
RSA 657:16, 26; RSA 659:27- a; HAVA Section 
703. 
Notice to Voters of Rejected Absentee
Ballot 
As best practice, but not required by law, the 
moderator or clerk should send all successfully 
challenged absentee voters a notice. Advise the 
voter that their absentee ballot was successfully 
challenged or was rejected by the moderator, and 
the grounds for the challenge or reason for 
rejection. 
Any person whose voter registration application 
was rejected shall be provided notice by the 
supervisors within seven days. RSA 657:16, 19, X. 
The moderator shall not unilaterally reject an 
absentee ballot for a challenge to the voter’s age, 
citizenship, or domicile without first obtaining a 
ruling from the supervisors of the checklist and 
completing a signed Asserting a Challenge form. 
RSA 659:27, 27-a. 
If the supervisors determine that, based on the 
challenge, the absentee voter is not qualified as a 
voter, following the election, the supervisors must 
initiate removal from the checklist by sending the 
voter a 30- day letter, except where there is an 
official notice of death, notice of transfer of voter 
registration, or notice of a permanent move out-of-
town from the USPS or Division of Motor Vehicles. 
Unlawful Use of Absentee Ballot 
Anyone who votes or attempts to vote in violation 
of any provision of N.H. RSA Chapter 657 – 
Absentee Voting – is guilty of a misdemeanor. This 
includes anyone who votes or attempts to vote 
under the provisions of RSA Chapter 657 who is 
not entitled to vote by absentee ballot. 
Election officials suspecting that a voter has voted 
using an absentee ballot when that voter was able 
and available to come to the polls and vote in 
person should notify the Attorney General’s Office. 
However, if the person’s absentee ballot otherwise 
satisfies the law and the voter is otherwise 
qualified to vote, the ballot must be cast and 
counted. 
A person loses their right to vote and have their 
vote counted only if the voter is an incarcerated 
felon or has been convicted of a willful violation of 
the election laws. New Hampshire Constitution, 
Part 1, Article 11; RSA 607-A:2. Therefore, it would 
violate the voter’s rights to refuse to count their 
ballot because of suspicion that they wrongfully 
used an absentee ballot when they were required 
by law to vote in person at the poll; it is important 
not to violate a person’s right to vote by not 
counting their ballot based on a mere suspicion 
that they are improperly voting absentee. 
A
DVERTISEMENTS ENCOURAGING THE USE OF AN 
ABSENTEE BALLOT 
Political parties and candidates sometimes 
promote voter turnout by sending out materials 
promoting voting by mail. New Hampshire only 
permits voting by absentee ballot for limited 
reasons, as defined by RSA 657:1. 
RSA 657:4, II requires that anyone promoting 
voting by absentee ballot in any advertising include 
a copy of the state application for an absentee 
ballot. The State issued absentee ballot request 
form contains a list of the lawful reasons that allow 
an individual to vote by absentee ballot. 
Clerks are directed to monitor the applications that 
come into their office. If pre -printed applications

political advertising but do not include the 
qualifications or requirements for voting absentee, 
immediately alert the Attorney General ’s Office. It 
is unlawful for anyone to vote or attempt to vote by 
absentee ballot who is not entitled to do so. RSA 
657:24. It is also unlawful for others, including 
campaigns, to conspire with others to violate this 
law. RSA 629:3. This procedure is intended to 
reduce the frequency of voters misled to believe 
they can vote absentee without justification. 
Processing Absentee Ballots on 
Election Day – Best Practices 
The key to processing absentee ballots is 
organization and starting early. 
An absentee voter should return a marked 
absentee ballot inside the affidavit envelope (form 
A), which has the absentee affidavit printed on it. 
That affidavit envelope must be placed inside the 
outer mailing envelope if the absentee ballot is 
returned by mail, however, if the absentee ballot is 
hand-delivered, the affidavit envelope containing 
the absentee ballot may be placed, but does not 
have to be placed, in the outer mailing envelope. 
Clerks will place a label on this outer envelope 
printed with the voter’s name, address, and voter 
ID number with a bar code for scanning. 
P
RE-ELECTION DAY: 
1. Organize returned absentee ballots with the 
attached voter’s absentee ballot application 
alphabetically by last name. In cities, or towns 
with districts, also organize the absentee 
ballots by ward/district. 
a. Separate returned absentee ballot 
envelopes that are marked “Not 
Registered” if the supervisors have not 
received the applications for absentee 
voter registration. 
2. On the final checklist which will be used at the 
election, highlight the names of voters who 
returned absentee ballot envelopes. SVRS will 
print the names of voters who requested 
absentee ballots in bold to help identify those 
voters when processing absentee ballots on 
election day. Absentee ballot requests 
received and entered into SVRS after the 
checklist is printed will not be bolded. 
3. At least 24 hours before the polls open, post 
the time when the polling location will: 
a. Cut open the absentee ballot outer 
envelopes without removing the affidavit 
envelope (for absentee ballots mailed in 
the outer envelopes); and 
b. Process absentee ballots. 
It is highly recommended to cut open the absentee 
ballot outer envelopes when polls open, which is 
the earliest allowable time. RSA 659:49-b. 
Absentee ballots are statutorily required to be 
processed at 1:00 p.m. unless a different time is 
posted and announced at least 24 hours before the 
polls open. The moderator of their designee must 
post the time at which the processing of absentee 
ballots shall begin at the polling place and one 
other public location at least 24 hours before the 
polls open. Additionally, when the polls open the 
moderator shall announce the time at which the 
processing of absentee ballots shall begin. RSA 
549:49. Processing must take place no earlier than 
two hours after the opening of the polls; for 
example, a polling place which opens at 8:00 a.m. 
can process absentee ballots no earlier than 10:00 
a.m. with proper notice. 
E
LECTION DAY: 
Processing an absentee ballot occurs within the 
rail in an area chosen by the moderator. The 
chosen area should be in a position where 
appointed party challengers and the public are 
able to observe processing and hear the 
moderator announce each voter’s name. The 
chosen area should not interfere with in- person 
voters checking in, using voting booths or privacy 
screens, and depositing their ballots in the ballot 
box or electronic ballot counting device. Only 
checking and marking the checklist, the final step 
before casting the absentee ballot, should occur at 
the check-in table(s).

voter’s signature and no name or

Any town that has adopted a municipal charter 
under RSA 49 -B:1-6 may hold elections on the 
second Tuesday in March, the second Tuesday in

November in odd-numbered years. RSA 669:1. 
Towns which adopt the provisions of RSA 40:13, 
known as Senate Bill 2 (“SB2”) towns, adopt 
separate dates for a deliberative meeting and an 
election day (official ballot voting day) where 
warrant articles are voted on by official ballot. The

City elections are held in accordance with

The state primary is held on the second Tuesday 
in September. RSA 653:8 (2026). Beginning in 
2028, the state primary will be held on the second

The state general election is held on the first

653:7. 
Presidential preference primaries shall be held on 
the second Tuesday in March or on a date selected 
by the Secretary of State which is seven days 
immediately preceding the date on which any other 
state shall hold a similar election, whichever is 
earlier, of each year in which a President of the 
United States is to be elected, or the year previous. 
The Secretary of State will call a special election if 
other than on the second Tuesday in March. RSA 
653:9. 
E
LECTION TIMES 
At all state elections the polls in both towns and 
cities shall open not later than 11 o'clock in the 
morning and may not close earlier than 7 o'clock 
in the evening. 
In cities, the city council shall determine the polling 
hours at least 30 days prior to the election. RSA 
659:4. 
At the 1994 general election, many communities 
voted yes on the following question: "Shall we 
adopt polling hours in (town name) at all state 
elections beginning with the 1996 state primary 
election under which the polls shall open not later 
than 8 o'clock in the morning?" If a community 
voted yes, then their polls must open at 8 a.m. for 
all state elections. This provision does not apply to 
local elections. 
Any town wishing to change their polling hours 
may do so by voting on an article at town meeting 
under the provisions of RSA 659:4-a. If the article 
passes, notify the Secretary of State. The 
Secretary of State will put the question regarding 
changing the hours on the next general election 
ballot in that town. 
The governing body of a town may extend the 
hours of polling in the town, provided that no 
extension of the hours of polling may take effect 
sooner than 60 days after its adoption. RSA 659:4-
a. 
For city elections, hours are set by city charter or 
by the city council. 
Polling hours for a town meeting or election shall 
be set by the selectmen or by a vote of the town. 
RSA 669:25. Municipalities are encouraged to 
have uniform polling places and hours to make it 
easy for voters to know when and where they vote 
at any election, state or municipal. 
Election Day Staff 
Moderator: The moderator is the chief election 
officer in charge of the polls and overseeing voting. 
RSA 659:9; RSA 44:12. 
Town Clerk: The town clerk has diverse municipal 
duties, including election responsibilities such as 
the warning of meetings, conducting elections, and 
reporting the results declared by the moderator. 
City Clerk: The city clerk has diverse municipal 
duties, including conducting elections. Check your 
local city charter for more details. 
Ward Clerk : The ward clerk has the powers, 
performs the duties, and is subject to the

RSA 44:12. 
Supervisors of the Checklist : Supervisors are 
responsible for registering voters; removing voters 
who permanently move, die, or otherwise are 
disqualified; and preparing, posting, revising, and 
certifying the checklist in their town or ward. In 
cities, these officials are often termed Registrars. 
Town Selectmen: Town selectmen are members 
of the governing body of a town who also have a 
variety of duties related to elections. 
Ward Selectmen: Ward selectmen generally have 
the same election- related powers, duties, and 
responsibilities that town selectmen have. RSA 
44:12. 
Inspector of Elections/Ballot Clerk: Ballot 
Clerks are Inspectors of Election or other election 
officials who check in voters and issue ballots. 
While the terms “ballot clerk” and “inspector of 
elections” are sometime used interchangeably, an 
“inspector of elections” may be assigned other 
duties. 
Greeter: An election official assigned by the 
moderator to assist and direct arriving voters to the 
correct starting place to register or vote. 
A
PPOINTMENT PROCESS FOR BALLOT CLERKS 
Effective January 1, 2028, the state chair of each 
of the two political parties that received the largest 
number of votes cast for governor at the prior 
general election may appoint inspectors of election 
to act at each polling place. By April 15 of each 
general election year, the Secretary of State shall 
provide to each chair a list of the number of 
inspectors of election that should be appointed for 
each town or ward. Each chair shall notify 
appointees and the town or ward clerk of such 
appointments between February 1 and April 30.  If 
such appointments are not made and noticed 
between February 1 and April 30, the town or ward 
selectmen shall appoint inspectors of election in 
equal number from the two political parties. 
Generally, there are at least two ballot clerks at 
each check -in station, one for each of the two 
major parties. The statute provides that if the 
number of voters at the polling place exceeds 
2000, the parties may appoint one additional 
inspector for each additional 1500 voters. RSA 
658:2. If the moderator so requests, the political 
parties may appoint on an equal basis an 
additional number of inspectors as the moderator 
deems necessary. RSA 658:2. 
The moderator chooses the ballot clerks from 
among the inspectors of election. Two ballot clerks 
are chosen, one from each political party for each 
check-in position (section of the checklist divided 
alphabetically so there are approximately equal 
numbers of voters in each section). Under the 
supervision of the moderator, the ballot clerks shall 
have charge of the ballots during the time the polls 
are open and shall furnish ballots to the voters. 
RSA 658:25; RSA 659:13. 
The inspectors who are not designated as ballot 
clerks are assigned duties by the moderator at the 
polling place, such as relieving the ballot clerks, 
greeting and assigning voters to appropriate lines, 
and assisting voters requiring assistance in 
marking their ballots. RSA 658:25; RSA 659:20. 
O
ATH OF OFFICE REQUIRED FOR ELECTION 
OFFICIALS 
Inspectors of elections (ballot clerks), appointed 
assistant election officials, moderators pro tem, 
supervisors pro tem, clerks pro tem, and 
selectmen pro tem, including anyone recruited to 
count ballots, shall take an oath of office before 
engaging in the duties of their position. A blank 
Oath of Office template is available in SVRS and 
the appendix. 
Officials administering an oath must file the 
completed Oath of Office forms with the clerk. RSA 
42:1; RSA 42:7; RSA 42:8; RSA 658:4. In addition 
to being a formal requirement of law, taking the 
oath of office helps ensure the individual 
understands that he or she is agreeing to fulfill the 
duties assigned by law to the office/position and 
that he or she will be subject to the consequences

Tasks to Complete Before the Polls 
Open 
PRE-ELECTION CERTIFICATE 
The Pre- Election Certificate is used for two 
purposes. 
Part I – Counting Ballots of the Pre- Election 
Certificate certifies that in accordance with RSA 
658:31-32, the ballots received by the clerk have 
been examined and counted, and requires the 
Moderator and Clerk to record and attest to the 
total number of Official Ballots (excluding 
Absentee and test ballots). This may be done at 
the time the ballots are inventoried. 
Part II – Electronic Ballot Counting Devices is 
applicable only to those polling locations which 
utilize an electronic ballot counting device. Part II 
requires the moderator and clerk to sign and certify 
on election day that “prior to placing the electronic 
ballot counting device or any memory device into 
service in an election, the moderator and the clerk 
[certified] that there is evidence that pre -election 
testing was conducted on each electronic ballot 
counting device and each memory device in the 
town or city’s possession, and that the[] ballot 
counting devices and memory devices have 
passed the test. Additionally, that all electronic 
ballot counting device seals are present, all seals 
have been maintained intact, and that any seals 
which have been broken in accordance with this 
section have been appropriately resealed and the 
activity log properly recorded and signed.” RSA 
656:42. The Pre -Election Certificate additionally 
requires the serial numbers of each electronic 
ballot counting device in use be recorded. 
I
NSPECT THE BALLOT COUNTING DEVICE 
In towns that use ballot counting devices, 
moderators must complete a few tasks before the 
polls officially open. In the presence of at least one 
witness, the moderator must inspect the ballot box 
and all its compartments to confirm the box is 
empty. 
P
RINT THE ZERO-TAPE/POLLS OPENED REPORT 
At this juncture, the device can be turned on. Upon 
powering the device, print what is called a “zero -
tape” which is essentially written/displayed proof 
that shows the starting count for each candidate 
and question is zero. Sign the zero tape /polls 
opened report and preserve it alongside the results 
tape (discussed later). Do not seal the zero-tape or 
results tape into the sealed ballot boxes —they 
should be retained by the clerk with the other non-
sealed election documentation. 
Polling Area Layout 
The polling area must be set up to provide an 
orderly flow of voters. Place the guardrails so that 
no person outside the rail can approach closer 
than 6 feet to the voting booths, voting privacy 
screens, or ballot counting device/ballot box. No 
person other than the election officials or registered 
voters in the process of voting may be within the 
rails except by the authority of the election officials. 
Ballots may not be removed from within the rail 
until sealed in storage boxes after the counting is 
completed. 
See page 62 for a model Traditional Polling Place 
Layout. 
See page 63 for a model Electronic P oll Book 
Polling Place Layout. 
G
REETERS 
The responsibilities of greeters are discussed 
more in depth in the Duties of Greeters section. 
The primary benefit of using greeters is to direct 
foot traffic into the polling place. The election day 
polling place has numerous tables, guardrails, 
election officials, and lines. Many individuals will 
be overwhelmed by navigating the maze, no 
matter how well organized it is. And it is not just 
voters entering the building: there may also be 
observers, challengers, state election officials, 
journalists, or even classroom students. Each of 
these folks must be directed to the proper area.

The other primary role of greeters is using the 
alpha voter list to check to see if a voter is already 
registered in order to direct the voter to the 
appropriate line (check-in or voter registration). 
Greeters can serve other useful purposes as well. 
A greeter at the polling place entrance can monitor 
for electioneering and ensure the no -
electioneering corridor is intact. Or, greeters 
placed near the ballot clerk table can help the 
ballot clerks ensure the number of voters within the 
guardrail does not exceed the number of voting 
booths/privacy screens. 
T
HE GUARDRAIL 
Every polling place must have a “guardrail” that 
segregates the voting area from the public. These 
rails can be rope, ribbon, or other materials. 
Place the guardrails so that no person outside the 
rail can approach closer than six feet to the voting 
booths, privacy screens, or ballot counting 
device/ballot box. RSA 658:9, I. No person other 
than election officials or registered voters in the 
process of voting may be within the rails except by 
authority of the election officials. RSA 659:21. 
Ballots may not be removed from within the rail 
until sealed in storage boxes after the counting is 
completed. RSA 659:38. Moderators must also 
ensure that the number of voters within the 
guardrail who have a ballot does not exceed the 
number of voting booths and privacy screens. RSA 
659:16. 
Placement of the guardrail must ensure that the 
voting booths and ballot counting device/ballot box 
are in plain view of those outside the guardrail. 
RSA 658:9, II. 
Certain rules also apply to the guardrail during 
counting (covered more fully in the Election Night 
section). Counting must be conducted within the 
guardrail, and no ballot can be placed within four 
feet of the guardrail during that time. RSA 659:63. 
O
BSERVATION AREA 
Polling places should also have designated 
observation areas. They fulfill two purposes. The 
first is for public viewing. Anyone can come and 
watch the casting and counting of ballots. This can 
include members of the public, political party 
representatives, or activist groups. Observers 
cannot, however, enter certain areas of the polling 
place. They cannot enter within the guardrail. RSA 
659:21. They cannot be within five feet of the voter 
registration table. RSA 654:7- c. They cannot be 
within six feet of the ballot clerk check -in table 
without moderator permission. RSA 659:13 -a. 
Creating one or more designated observation area 
ensures these rules are followed. 
The second reason for defined observation areas 
relates to challengers. Challengers are individuals 
who may challenge a voter’s qualification to vote. 
The challenge process will be discussed more fully 
later in this section. For layout purposes, it is 
important to ensure that challengers can hear 
ballot clerks announce the names of voters 
checking-in, RSA 654:7-c, and to see and hear the 
hand counting of ballots/have a line of sight on any 
ballot counting device. RSA 654:7 -c; RSA 666:5. 
Creating an observation area allows moderators to 
ensure these requirements are met. Note that in 
some polling places, the normal observation area 
may not be close enough for the challengers to 
hear the ballot clerks announce the names of 
voters. In that situation, a separate challenger area 
will need to be created closer to the checklist. 
S
UPERVISOR OF THE CHECKLIST TABLE 
One of the first tables a voter comes across should 
be the Supervisors of the Checklist . New 
Hampshire permits same day voter registration, so 
placing the Supervisors near the entrance allows 
for a clean traffic flow. The supervisors are also 
present for situations where registered voters 
changed their name and thus cannot check -in 
initially. For more information on voter registration, 
see section I. 
On election day, the supervisors are permitted to 
appoint assistant supervisors who can register 
voters. RSA 658:7. The Secretary of State’s Office 
allows towns to give one assistant supervisor 
limited SVRS access. They can enter new voters,

make changes to voters, and put voters in pending 
removal status. They cannot approve or remove 
voters. 
Usually, individuals who register on election day 
desire to vote upon registering. After the 
supervisors process and approve a qualified 
individual’s registration, the person then proceeds 
to the ballot clerk table to check -in and obtain a 
ballot. The ball ot clerks will either have the 
physical checklist or electronic poll books that will 
not have the newly registered voter. As such, the 
supervisors (upon registering the person) must 
notify the ballot clerks to add the person to the 
checklist and mark them as having obtained a 
ballot. 
In towns that do not use electronic poll books, this 
is done using a New Voter Authorization Form. A 
copy of this form is in SVRS Help Instructions and 
the appendix. The form is completed by the newly 
registered voter, signed by a supervisor of the 
checklist, and then handed to the ballot clerk. The 
ballot clerk will add the person’s name to the 
checklist and issue them a ballot. 
For towns that use electronic poll books, some 
towns use this same process, while others will 
have their supervisors use an electronic poll book 
to add election- day voter registrants to the 
checklist. Upon a supervisor entering the new 
voter into the poll book, the machine will generate 
a green receipt with the voter’s name on it. The 
voter can take this green receipt to the ballot clerks 
which will alert them that the person is a newly 
registered voter. Towns can still use the New Voter 
Authorization Form alongside or in place of green 
receipts—what matters is that each polling place 
has a process for notifying the ballot clerks that an 
individual is newly registered and must be added 
to the checklist before obtaining a ballot. This 
ensures that during rec onciliation the numbers of 
voters who checked in matches the number of 
ballots. 
For more information on how ballot clerks must 
add a new voter to the checklist, see the detailed 
ballot clerk procedures in SVRS Help Instructions. 
At primaries, undeclared voters may, after 
declaring a party and voting, complete the 
"Undeclared Voters Election Day Party Affiliation 
Change Form” or sign the “Undeclared Voters Re-
Registration" list at the polls to return to undeclared 
status on election day. This is another reason why 
the supervisors of the checklist table must be 
outside the guardrail —voters cannot re- enter it 
upon having voted. 
B
ALLOT CLERK TABLE 
As the name implies, ballot clerks issue ballots. 
Before doing so, they must check the registered 
voter in (or add the newly registered voter to the 
checklist, discussed above). Voters must present 
identification to be checked in. For more 
information on acceptable identification, see the 
Duties of Ballot Clerks section. 
New Hampshire law does not set minimum 
standards for the number of check -in stations the 
way it does for voting booths. Based on experience 
and research, it is prudent to have at least one 
check-in station for every expected 600 in person 
voters. For high- volume polling places, it is 
important to break the checklist into sections, 
allowing more than one voter to check in 
simultaneously. 
A breakdown of the optimal distribution of letters 
based on the number of check -in stations is 
located in the appendix and in SVRS Help 
Instructions. 
Towns that do not use electronic poll books to 
check voters in will do so using the paper checklist. 
The paper checklist contains the names, 
addresses, voter identification number, and 
political affiliation of every registered voter in that 
town or ward. Once the ballot clerks check the 
person in by marking the checklist, they hand the 
voter a ballot or some type of receipt/token used to 
obtain a ballot from another ballot clerk. 
The process looks different for towns that use 
electronic poll books. Although the law permits 
towns and cities to use electronic poll books for 
voter check -in, it requires them to continue

marking the paper checklist in parallel, with a lag 
time of no more than 30 minutes of a voter 
checking in. To facilitate marking the checklist, the 
poll books print a white receipt after each voter 
checks in. This receipt is collected by the ballot 
clerk who gives the voter a ballot. That receipt is 
then used by ballot clerks to mark the paper 
checklist. 
Some towns have reported that the marking 
process can be sped up by assigning some ballot 
clerks to alphabetize the receipts before 
transferring the receipts to other ballot clerks who 
are responsible for marking the checklist. 
As a final note, t o prevent voters from marking 
ballots in public or trying to leave the area within 
the guardrail with a ballot, moderators should 
require the ballot clerks to hand out ballots only 
when a voting booth/screen is available. RSA 
659:13; RSA 659:14. Some moderators will 
employ additional greeters to assist the ballot 
clerks in monitoring the number of available voting 
booths. 
W
HERE TO PROCESS ABSENTEE BALLOTS 
Process absentee ballots within the guardrail in an 
area that will not interfere with in- person voters. 
Allow appointed party challengers and the public 
to observe processing from outside the rail in a 
position where they can hear the moderator’s 
announcement of each voter’s name. RSA 659:50. 
At most polling places, the moderator can process 
absentee ballots one at a time, however, if a polling 
place has a high volume of absentee ballots to 
process, the moderator may appoint deputy or 
assistant moderators to simultaneously process 
batches of absentee ballots. 
For more information on the processing of 
absentee ballots, see both the Absentee Ballots 
section and Duties of Moderators section. 
V
OTING BOOTHS AND EQUIPMENT 
As more fully covered in the Duties of Selectmen 
section (as selectmen are responsible for 
equipping the polling place), the number of voting 
booths and privacy screens provided at the polling 
place depends on the number of voters on the 
checklist and the type of the election. See that 
section for more information on calculating the 
number of booths and screens. 
S
POILED BALLOTS 
A voter who makes a mistake when marking his or 
her ballot may spoil his ballot by taking it to the 
moderator. Any voter who spoils a ballot(s) may 
receive a replacement, not exceeding three in all, 
upon returning the spoiled ballot(s) to the 
moderator. 
The moderator must write the word "canceled" on 
the spoiled ballot and sign it. It is important during 
the counting process and at any recount to be able 
to clearly identify marked ballots that were spoiled 
and not cast and therefore must not be counted. 
The moderator must hold spoiled ballots aside and 
properly account for t hem on the post -election 
certificate. Seal spoiled ballots, ideally in a 
separate envelope marked “spoiled ballots,” with 
the other unused ballots at the end of counting. 
RSA 659:22. 
C
HECK-OUT TABLE FOR HAND-COUNT TOWNS 
In hand -count towns, the clerk or an assistant 
staffs a checklist located just before the ballot box. 
As a voter arrives to hand his or her ballot to the 
moderator for casting into the ballot box, the voter 
checks out with the clerk. The photo identificati on 
requirements for check -in do not apply to 
checkout, otherwise the process is the same as 
check-in. The voter states his or her name (name 
and party, if a primary) and is checked out. If the 
voter was registered as undeclared when they 
arrived at the polling place, they should be given 
an opportunity to sign the list or complete the form 
to return to undeclared. 
D
EPOSITING COMPLETED BALLOT – HAND COUNT 
Before leaving the voting booth or voting privacy 
screen in a hand- count polling place, the voter 
shall fold their ballot in the same way it was folded 
when received by them and shall keep it folded so 
that the marks on it cannot be seen. They shall

then proceed to the checkout table and shall 
announce their name to the town clerk who shall 
repeat the name and place a mark beside it on the 
checklist. The voter shall then present his ballot 
with the official endorsement uppermost to the 
moderator who shall then deposit the ballot in the 
ballot box. 
D
EPOSITING COMPLETED BALLOT – B ALLOT 
COUNTING DEVICE 
Towns that have ballot counting devices differ from 
hand-count towns in a few ways. First, there are 
no check -out tables, so voters proceed directly 
from the voting booth to the ballot counting device. 
Second, the ballots are not folded. To protect the 
voter’s privacy, state law requires polling places to 
provide privacy folders for voters to use when 
carrying the marked ballot to the device. A manilla 
folder or large piece of paper can be used as a 
privacy folder. 
The size of the folder is important because the goal 
is to maintain the secrecy of how the voter marked 
the ballot. It must be of sufficient size to cover the 
area of the ballot containing offices, questions, and 
ovals. Ideally, it will be sized so the top or bottom 
edge of the ballot protrudes, allowing the voter to 
feed the ballot into the device without removing the 
ballot from the folder. Some municipalities utilize 
extra-long ballots in their local elections, so ensure 
that the privacy folders are long enough in those 
elections. 
The privacy folder is turned in once the ballot is fed 
into the ballot counting device. Because the folders 
can be recycled back to the ballot-issuing table as 
soon as the voter feeds his or her ballot into the 
ballot counting device, it is not necessary t o have 
a folder for every ballot printed. Depending on the 
size of your community, typically one privacy folder 
for every voting booth and voting privacy screen 
will be sufficient. 
Third, the voter feeds the marked ballot into the 
device. Election officials do not handle the ballot 
unless it must be placed into the side pocket. 
Every ballot counting device has a side pocket — 
an auxiliary compartment on the side of the 
machine that ballots can be manually fed into. 
They are covered more fully below. 
W
HEN TO USE THE SIDE POCKET – OVERVOTES AND 
HAND-COUNT REQUESTS 
All ballot counting devices have a side 
compartment, sometimes referred to as an 
auxiliary compartment or side pocket. The primary 
function of the side pocket is for overvoted ballots. 
New Hampshire law requires the ballot counting 
devices be programmed to reject ballots when a 
ballot contains more than the allowable number of 
votes for an office or ballot question. RSA 656:42, 
XI. This is known as an “overvote.” When the 
machine rejects an overvoted ballot, the voter 
must be instructed to place the ballot in the side 
pocket to be hand counted later. If it is an absentee 
ballot, the moderator or their appointee places the 
overvoted ballot in the side pocket. 
Naturally, voters may ask why their ballot was 
rejected, or why it is being inserted into the side 
pocket. Best practice is to tell them that the device 
could not read their ballot and it will therefore be 
hand counted. A voter may, however, treat the 
ballot as a spoiled ballot and request a new one. 
In that case, follow the process for spoiled ballots 
(discussed above). 
Use caution when interacting with a voter whose 
ballot has been returned to the voter due to the 
device reading an overvote. Even if asked by the 
voter, best practice is to avoid looking at how the 
ballot is marked to try to find the overvoted race(s). 
Even if that voter is willing to give up their right to 
a secret ballot, others hearing or seeing the 
interaction may view it as election official 
misconduct. 
Other than for overvoted ballots, the side pocket is 
used for voters who request their ballot be hand 
counted and for UOCAVA ballots. Any voter may 
request their ballot be hand counted. RSA 656:42, 
XII. Voters that request their ballots be hand 
counted must hand it to the election official 
manning the device, who will place it in the side

pocket. 
UOCAVA ballots must be accepted no matter what 
paper they are printed on and, accordingly, must 
be placed in the side pocket. 
BALLOT SUPPLY DEPLETED 
The clerk must set aside at least one of each page 
and type of official ballots in use at an election for 
use to make copies if necessary. 
If the supply of official ballots is exhausted, the 
clerk must first use leftover absentee ballots. The 
clerk should cross out the word “absentee” and 
initial the absentee ballot before the ballot clerk 
issues it to a voter. 
If the supply of official ballots and absentee ballots 
is exhausted, the town or city clerk shall prepare 
additional unofficial ballots as provided in RSA 
659:24 and RSA 658:35. Photocopies must be 
made of an unused official ballot. Each photocopy 
is authenticated by the clerk or their deputy clerk, 
signing their name or initials prior to issuing the 
photocopied ballot to a voter. A clerk may also use 
a signature stamp to authenticate photocopies of 
ballots. Authentication distinguishes any such 
authorized unofficial ballots from fraudulently 
created ballots. RSA 659:24. Keep an accurate 
record of the number of unofficial ballots created 
and the number put into use as election day 
ballots. The moderator requires this number for the 
ballot inventory on the moderator’s Post- Election 
Certificate. 
Generally, use at least ten such ballots. If fewer 
than ten unofficial ballots are needed, void any 
procedure that would make the ballot(s) used by 
the last few voters identifiable. Preserve the right 
to a secret ballot. 
A
CCESSIBLE VOTING SYSTEM – THE OMNIBALLOT 
TABLET 
Every city, town, and school district with an official 
ballot system is required to equip each polling 
place with at least one accessible voting system. 
This applies to all elections —federal, state, local, 
and special elections. 
In 2025, the Secretary of State’s Office purchased 
new AVS devices from Democracy Live called the 
OmniBallot tablet. The State is responsible and 
bears the cost for programming state/federal 
elections, RSA 659:20- b, III(d), while local 
jurisdictions are responsible for configuring the 
devices for local elections. RSA 659:20-b, I(b). The 
programming cost is $650 for each election per 
jurisdiction. 
The Secretary of State’s Office and Democracy 
Live coordinated in early 2026 to deliver the 
devices, printers, and all peripherals to all towns 
and cities, who will store them permanently. They 
will not be returned to the State, as was done with 
the prior system. 
At the polling place, the OmniBallot tablet must be 
placed in the accessible voting booth provided by 
the Secretary of State for that purpose. RSA 658:9, 
III. This booth is ideally set up near the moderator’s 
post by the ballot box/ballot counting device to 
permit the moderator to readily receive the ballot 
by hand in a privacy sleeve. In addition to the 
privacy tent, you should also have a table, lamp, 
and magnifier screen to use with the OmniBallot 
tablet. 
The OmniBallot system must be tested prior to 
each election. If you are a machine counting 
device town and you haven't tested your device, 
you must test them together following the guide to 
marking a test deck. If you have already tested 
your device or are a hand count town, then test 
upon receipt of your marking file and ballots. 
Turn on and test the OmniBallot before the polls 
open. Check the tablet regularly throughout the 
day. If the screen is dark during an election, the 
system may have not been turned on as required. 
The OmniBallot must be set up and available for 
use by all voters in all elections. No voter is 
required to disclose their disability in order to use 
the OmniBallot. Any voter may use the machine, 
regardless of disability status, upon request. Do 
NOT ask a voter what disability they have, or why

can be found in SVRS Help Instructions. 
V
OTER REQUESTING ASSISTANCE MARKING A 
BALLOT 
A voter requiring assistance with marking his or her 
ballot must first declare to the moderator that he or 
she cannot mark the ballot without assistance. The 
moderator must make the voter aware of the 
option to vote privately and independently using 
the accessible ballot marking system. If the voter 
nonetheless prefers assistance, the moderator 
arranges the assistance. The voter may choose 
the assistance of a ballot clerk or a person of the 
voter’s choosing. However, the voter may not 
choose the voter’s employer or union official. RSA 
659:20; 52 U.S.C. §10508. 
Both the person requesting assistance and the 
person providing assistance must then complete 
the following oaths (a template of the following 
oaths is available in the appendix): 
• 
o 
• 
o 
The Voter: 
I, ____, do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I 
am unable to mark a ballot and require 
assistance in voting. 
The Individual Assisting the Voter: 
I, ____, do solemnly swear (or affirm) that 
in providing assistance to ____ (the voter), 
I shall mark the ballot as directed by 
him/her and will not unduly influence 
his/her decision with respect to selecting 
any candidate or issue presented on the 
ballot and that I shall thereafter give no 
information regarding same. 
S
ETTING UP AN ADDITIONAL POLLING PLACE 
Voting procedures at the additional polling place 
are the same as at the central polling location. RSA 
658:33; RSA 658:16. A few other notes: 
• 
• 
Two copies of a certified copy of the 
supervisor's checklist for the area served by 
that additional polling place must be given to 
the clerk before the election. 
On the day of the election, the clerk must bring 
the copies of the checklist as prepared and 
certified by the supervisors and deposited with 
him or her to the additional polling site. 
• The clerk is also responsible for providing a 
sufficient number of ballots for the additional 
polling place. The preparation of this package 
is done in the presence of the moderator and 
selectmen, and it is then delivered to the 
assistant moderator at the additional polling 
place by two election officers designated by the 
moderator. 
Timing for Processing Absentee 
Ballots 
Process absentee ballots before any counting of 
election day ballots takes place. The moderator 
must announce in a loud voice so that everyone in 
the hall can hear that he or she is about to begin 
processing the absentee ballots. 
Generally, processing absentee ballots begins at 
1:00 p.m. unless the moderator chooses a different 
time. RSA 659:49, I. Processing of absentee 
ballots may begin at a different time no earlier than 
two hours after the opening of the polls. The 
moderator, or designee, shall post the time at 
which the processing of absentee ballots shall 
begin at the polling place and one other public 
location at least 24 hours before the polls open. 
RSA 659:49, II. In addition, when the polls open, 
the moderator shall announce the time at which 
the processing of absentee ballots shall begin. 
Process any absentee ballots received in the mail, 
after the start time for processing absentee ballots 
and prior to 5 p.m. on the day of the election, as 
soon after receipt as possible. No ballots may ever 
be hand counted before the polls close: device 
counted ballots may be inserted into the ballot 
counting device. RSA 659:49; RSA 659:49-b; RSA 
659:50. 
Challenge of a Voter 
A challenge is the challenge of a voter’s 
qualification to vote. This section will cover who 
can assert a challenge, when and where it can be

asserted, and how the process works. 
WHO CAN ASSERT A CHALLENGE? 
There are four different types of individuals 
permitted to submit challenges: 
• Any registered voter from the town or ward in 
question. RSA 659:27. 
• Election officials. RSA 659:27. 
• A challenger appointed by a political 
committee. RSA 666:4. 
• A challenger appointed by the Attorney 
General. RSA 666:5. 
W
HEN AND WHERE ARE CHALLENGES ASSERTED? 
Challenges to an in- person voter’s qualification 
occur at the ballot clerk check -in table before a 
voter receives a ballot. As noted in the layout 
section above, challengers have a statutory right 
to see and hear each voter as they check -in. It is 
therefore important to ensure there is an area for 
challengers near the ballot clerk table but not 
within the guardrail. The easiest solution is to place 
a designated observation area for both general 
observers and challengers near the ballot clerk 
table. 
Challenges to absentee ballots occur during the 
processing of absentee ballots. A qualified 
challenger must make a challenge immediately 
after the moderator announces an absentee 
voter’s name. As noted in the absentee ballot 
section, moderators should process absentee 
ballots in an area where challengers can see and 
hear. For this reason, it is typically done behind the 
guardrail but near the observation area. 
P
ERMISSIBLE REASONS FOR CHALLENGING A 
VOTER’S QUALIFICATIONS 
A person asserting a challenge can do so based 
on one of several bases: 
•
 
• 
• 
The 
voter is not the individual whose name he 
or she gave to the ballot clerk; 
The voter already voted in the election; 
The voter is disqualified as having been 
convicted of treason, bribery, or a willful 
violation of election laws; 
•
 
• 
• 
• 
• 
• 
• 
The v
oter is not 18 years or older; 
The voter is not a United States citizen; 
The voter is not domiciled in the town/ward; 
The voter does not reside at the address listed 
for that person on the checklist; 
The voter is an incarcerated felon; 
The voter is attempting to vote in a primary and 
is not a declared member of that party; 
The voter is ineligible pursuant to some other 
legal justification under state or federal law. 
HOW DOES THE CHALLENGE PROCESS WORK FOR 
IN-PERSON VOTERS? 
A challenger must be a registered voter from the 
town/ward, an election official, or an appointed 
challenger with a signed letter from either the party 
chair or Attorney General. A qualified challenger 
who wants to make a challenge must notify the 
moderator and identify the voter being challenged. 
The moderator must afford the challenger a 
reasonable opportunity to complete the “Asserting 
a Challenge” form but may want to discuss the 
basis for the challenge first. 
Instruct both the challenger and the voter to talk 
directly to the moderator, not each other. In some 
cases, explaining the law may make a formal 
challenge unnecessary. Either the voter may learn 
that he or she should be voting at a different polling 
place, or the challenger may learn that their basis 
for challenging is not sufficient or accurate. To the 
extent necessary, the moderator may ask the voter 
and the challenger to step aside to allow those in 
line to proceed with checking in and voting. To 
proceed with a formal challenge, the challenger 
must complete the form and swear or affirm, under 
penalties of perjury, the grounds cited as the basis 
of the challenge. 
If the ground for the challenge (including 
challenges to absentee voters) is age, citizenship, 
or domicile, the moderator must ask the 
supervisors of the checklist to rule whether the 
challenged voter is either qualified or not qualified. 
The moderator rules on challenges based on all 
other grounds.
